en: The Later Moonlight on the Siddhāntas of Śrī Vīraśaiva.

Within the interior of the temple of the Śrī-Cintāmaṇi, seated upon the tip of the Brahma-throne, one should joyfully meditate with delight on the goddess Bhramarāmbikā—she who dwells on the lap of the illustrious Malleśa-Śiva, whose complexion is like vermilion and whose garments are of that same hue; she who holds a bow as radiant as a cluster of Puṇḍra sugarcane, an elephant-goad, a noose, and arrows of flowers; and she who bears the crescent moon upon her head and possesses three eyes.
In the garden of my mind, I remember the auspicious Ambika, who is like a female bee upon a blossoming jasmine creeper enveloped by the splendor of Śrī Malli.

I worship the young girl who rests her lute upon the jeweled ornaments placed above her jar-like breasts, who is languid with intoxication, and whose topknot is set upon the dark lap [of her father]. She is the beloved of Malla, the destroyer of pride, the daughter of Vyāsa, Guha, and the one who dwells in the anthill.
I bow to her who embodies the threefold form of the *liṅga*, through the beloved bonds of speech.
In the courtyard of the temple, I beheld that Ambikā united with Maheśa—
she who is as fickle as lightning, yet the supreme embodiment of the highest light.
I bow to the Śrī Mallikārjuna Liṅga, the life-liṅga on Strīgiri,
especially for the sake of the Śrī Vīraśaivas and the Siddhas.
Udbhavārādhya was the son of Vaṃśordhacandraśekhara;
his son was Annapūrṇāsu, and Vīrabhadrārādhya was a knower of the Tantras.
Endowed with the threefold marks within the three bodies, beginning with the cause,
he— who was of the Bhāradvāja gotra and had been worshipped by his ancestors as Malleśa—
having thoroughly examined the Śiva scriptures, extracted the essential meaning in every respect.
"Contemplating within my heart the venerable Gadheṇendra, I shall briefly expound the *Śrīmatsiddhāntottarakaumudī*, which is appropriate for Vīraśaivas."
Whenever indeed there occurred a decline of Dharma,
at that very time Gaṇeśa manifested his descent upon the surface of the earth.
Thus, in the Śrīśaṅkha-saṃhitā,
it was spoken by the great-souled Śrī Śaṅkara himself to the high-minded Ṣaṇmukha.
Those born from a portion of that Lord of Gaṇas are known as Vīraśaivas;
for them, the initiation that effects the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), called "Consisting of Consciousness" (cinmaya), is now described.
The wearing of the *liṅga* has been declared as that which resides at the pinnacle of all the Vedas;
the worship of the glorious *liṅga*, together with the daily rites, has been proclaimed.
Their meditative absorption (samādhi) has been described in the auspicious world of Kālāgni;
I shall explain all these in sequence here through the sacred scriptures (śruti).
In this regard, first the majesty of the illustrious lords of the Gaṇas is now proclaimed—
in that mine of all Śiva-dharmas, which is an abode of auspiciousness.
This *Rudrādhyāya*, which is praised by even the five Rudras and is destructive of sins, has been mastered; salutations to the Lord of Paths (*pathīnām pataye*).
Thus the mantra has been fully explained; within it, three paths are traditionally taught:
the southern, the northern, and the third, in due order.
The path of smoke, the path of flame, and so forth, and the third is the path of devotion;
eighty-eight thousand sages are intent upon the path of action.
An equal number of great-souled sages, who are highly exalted and firmly established in Brahman, engage themselves in the two divisions of ritual action and spiritual knowledge.
Likewise, in the section on devotion, there are great lords of the hosts,
numbering in the thousands upon thousands, beyond counting.
The hosts of attendants of the God, whose Vedic conduct is well-known, are invoked by such mantras as "Namo vaḥ kirikebhyaśca."
When, by means of the mantra "Just as one might [cover] space with a hide," supreme devotion directed solely toward Śiva becomes ever greater.
Born with devotion to Him as their inner core, they proceed upon His path;
[this occurs] due to the differentiations of devotion within the power of the lords of sages.
Creation arose perfectly from Śiva, specifically as half of him;
those who are liberated possess that which is indeed considered the supreme material *vibhūti*.
Those who know the secret understand another, supreme, non-material [vibhūti] to be the most secret.
Thus was it said of old by Upamanyu, even though he was great, regarding Kṛṣṇā; and when that matter had been explained by Śiva, his passion for her ceased.
By the will of Śiva, she creates innumerable cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) through the essence of Śiva’s power;
indeed, this great creation is her most profound secret.
She gives birth to all the lords of the Gaṇas, who are produced from the essence of devotion to Śiva.
Just as the flame of a great fire, when divided, takes the form of a lamp,
so too the power of Maheśvara, when divided, takes the form of devotion.
Since the flame is enveloped in darkness while the lamp is brilliantly luminous,
therefore power (*śakti*) is considered to be accompanied by latent impressions (*savāsanā*), whereas devotion (*bhakti*) is regarded as being free from latent impressions (*nirvāsanā*).
Devotion is most great, pure, extremely subtle, beautiful, and supreme;
it consists of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Power (śakti) is said to be activity (pravṛtti), while devotion (bhakti) is declared to be cessation (nivṛtti). Through power, the creation of the phenomenal world occurs; through devotion, its dissolution is held to take place.
The power (śakti) is downward-facing, while devotion (bhakti) is upward-facing;
that is declared to be the power of illusion (māyā-śakti), whereas devotion is said to be free from illusion (nirmāyā).
Indeed, due to the diversity of [divine] power, that which is formless assumes form;
likewise, due to the diversity of devotion, that which is formless has been described by me as having form.
In the investigation of ultimate reality, there is no difference between power (*śakti*) and devotion (*bhakti*).
Even by means of logic and valid cognition, devotion is superior to the qualities of devotion;
that devotion arises solely from grace, and grace is born of devotion.
Just as the seed is from the sprout, or as the sprout is from the seed,
so too is Brahman alone— the eternal, full, consciousness-bliss, whose nature is existence.
Whatever indeed may be the form of the Indestructible, that is declared to be devotion (bhakti).
Born with devotion to Him as their inner core, these devotees of Śiva are identical with Śiva;
they are uniquely endowed with the knowledge of Śiva and are solely intent upon meditation on Śiva.
Constantly engaged in the contemplation of Śiva-yoga, ever devoted to the worship of Śiva,
endowed with single-minded dedication to Śiva, and intent upon devotion to Śiva.
United with the limbs of Śiva’s Liṅga, they are the fires of Śiva’s consciousness;
united with the Liṅga in every limb, they are solely devoted to meditation upon Śiva.
Filled with the grace of Śiva, always devoted to the mantras of Śiva,
having no other refuge, those virtuous ones are dedicated to the conduct of Śiva.
Devoted to the observance of Śiva’s vows, upholders of Śiva’s dharma,
rejoicing in Śiva’s grace, they themselves experience the power of the Liṅga.
Those who are endowed with the conduct of Śiva, who delight in conversation concerning Śiva,
who are perfected in the Brahman of the six locations (ṣaṭsthala), and who shine with the half of half of the six steps (ṣaṭpadārdhārdha).
Perfectly endowed with the reality of the six chakras, they follow the path that transcends the six realms;
all of them offer salutations to one another, speak kindly to one another,
are joined as servants to one another, and delight in embracing one another.
Endowed with infinite power, possessing infinite strength and valor,
they are invested with supreme sovereignty and possessed of infinite splendor.
They possess infinite and wondrous conduct; they perform infinite and wondrous deeds;
they are mounted upon infinite vehicles; and they have reached the further shore of infinite scripture.
Possessing infinite scriptural knowledge and omniscience, they are the embodiments of infinite bliss.
They are knowers of all infinite scriptures, possessing infinite subtle forms;
they are omniscient, complete in every respect, and uniquely worshiped by all the worlds.
Endowed with all sovereign qualities, they are the graspers who bestow grace upon all;
[they perform] creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and supreme grace.
And by the command of Śiva, these perform the fivefold functions;
they are the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, endowed with a thousand eyes and feet.
Their hands, numbering in the thousands, were filled with thousands of arrows;
they were seated upon divine lion-thrones and possessed bodies of celestial form.
Likewise, there were other hosts of Maheśvara with various faces,
endowed with divine ornaments and anointed with divine ashes.
Four-armed and three-eyed, they are experts in the Śaiva Siddhānta;
resembling pure crystal, they wear matted hair and the crescent moon.
Established in the union of that essential harmony and surrounded by the Lord of All,
there are thousands of innumerable Rudras who are distinguished by their specific functions.
"It is remembered [in scripture] and is not seen [in common experience]; understand this indeed.

Thus is described the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*) for the Vīraśaivas who have arisen from the creation of Śiva and possess the various classes of *liṅgas*. [This is followed by: "The wearing [of the *liṅga*]."
The auspicious body of the sage Śrīparvata, which was situated upon the broad summit.
I do not worship Maheśvara, who is praised as the sole knower by the multitude of those worthy of praise;
nor do I worship the Mandāra and Kalpa creepers, which are clusters of the thirty-six principles.
One should take refuge in Ambikā, who is like a bee at the edge of the fruit of dualistic action,
as well as in those previously mentioned Śaivas who are devoted to the duties of Śiva.
Indeed, the regulation of the duties of the castes and stages of life is considered to be twofold: one was established by Śiva and spoken by Brahmā in ancient times;
the other, however, is the steadfast adherence to the duties spoken by Śiva for those who practice the Śiva-āśrama.
"The Dharma of the Grandfather (Brahmā) is prescribed for those devoid of the Śiva-saṃskāras.
Having thus examined the scriptures and extracted their essence,
I shall now describe the stage of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga, which is appropriate for Vīraśaivas.
"It destroys the suffering and sins of saṃsāra, directly bestows liberation, is auspicious, is conjoined with daily rites, and is the sole means for divine awakening.

Now, one might object: "For Vīraśaivas, the worship of the *liṅga* alone constitutes knowledge in the form of the union between the *liṅga* and the body (*liṅgāṅgasambandha*), and so forth, without exception."

In the Śaiva Siddhāntas, it is declared that [the worship] must be performed joined with daily ritual (*dinakarman*); for it is said: "That [worship] should indeed be performed conjoined with daily ritual. If one asks what the fruit of daily ritual is, we reply to that: in the *Śaivasiddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*, it is stated: "By means of knowledge conjoined with right conduct (*ācāra*), Maheśvara does not abandon [the devotee]; therefore, through the excellence of conduct, [liberation occurs] even upon the falling away of the body."
Even when knowledge has been perfected, action is still appropriate for the wise;
therefore, one should not abandon action that is free from attachment to its fruits.
A mere fragment of right conduct serves as an ornament for all.
A person devoid of proper conduct is censured in the world;
for knowledge and action are mutually dependent, like a blind man and a lame man.
Therefore, those who are dispassionate toward the arising of phenomena should practice non-duality;
for fire does not manifest without the friction of the kindling sticks.
Likewise, without ritual action, there would be no internal illumination that is Śiva; for as long as He is not known, behold how the Lord does not become gracious.
"One should perform one's duties in such a way that they are in accordance with the authoritative scriptures.
It is also stated in the latter part of the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*: "Those who, while performing the duty prescribed for their own caste, offer worship..."
Those men who, abandoning the ritual injunctions prescribed for their own caste, constantly worship Śrīkaṇṭha with devotion, are also known as Māheśvaras.
The Lord does not accept the worship of those who worship Śiva [alone];
the conduct of the castes and stages of life was previously proclaimed by Śiva.
Those who disregard them and violate the command of Śiva shall receive the same punishment that is meted out to men who disobey the king's order.
For humans who violate the command of Śiva, hell is indeed the punishment.
Having abandoned the Dharma enjoined by Śambhu through Sāmba, whoever worships Śiva [otherwise],
Śiva becomes angry with him on account of his violation of His own command.
He who does not abandon the Dharma characterized by awakening as commanded by Śiva,
and who worships Śaṅkara, to him Sāmba becomes gracious.
When the Lord of Gods, Sadāśiva, the Great Bliss, is pleased,
what indeed is difficult for a mortal to achieve within the three worlds? [This applies] when Mahādeva, the supreme among the most compassionate, is the Great Bliss.
Whether he be a fool or a wise man, one whose mind is serene is liberated.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining grace from Śiva, the Supreme Self,
the wise person should perform the obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas and Smṛtis, as if they were His command.
Maheśvara should always perform the twilight worship at the three junctions of the day;
for the Sun is the primary body of Bhīma, the Supreme Self.
Whoever performs its worship becomes one who has performed the worship of Śiva. One should worship that which clings to the Liṅga and the limbs during all three junctions of time (saṃdhyā).
That saṃdhyā gives birth to the universe; she is indeed beyond Māyā and partless (niṣkalā).
The Sovereign is the absolute Power, who has arisen from the three principles;
she is the Dharma proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti, which rests upon the obligatory and occasional rites.
He who, having fashioned [an image], worships Śambhu is remembered as a sāttvika devotee;
he who is sāttvika, wears the liṅga, and performs the daily rites according to the rules.
He is said to be the beloved devotee of the blue-throated god.
Thus, for the benefit of practitioners engaged in the duties of the four stages of life, I shall explain the Krama, beginning with the Nitya rites, according to the procedure for awakening the Krama.
Fifteen auspicious muhūrtas are proclaimed for the time of night;
here, the fourteenth muhūrta is known by the name Brahma.
In that state of supreme bliss, one who is pure should meditate upon Śaṅkara in the mind;
one should behold the Guru as the moving Śiva and never look away from them.
Then, having departed from his house, he should go outside without weariness;
[he should walk] a distance of one *vikṣepa* on the surface of the earth.
The wise man should place his sacred thread (upavīta) either on his hand or at the root of his ear;
facing south at night and facing north during the day. He should avoid facing the sun when performing rites with water and the like, as well as when facing the moon, a cow, or a Brahmin.
Near a temple, at a well, in a cow-pen, on ashes, in a field,
in the shade of a tree, in a river, and within a lake.
A man should not perform either [of these acts] near a tree belonging to the Daityas, on the shore of the great ocean, at a crossroads, or in the middle of a house.
When the evacuation is finished, the destroyer of fatigue, having cast off his garment,
should cover the ground with grass while discharging excrement and urine.
According to the *Suprabheda*, having grasped the penis with the left hand and a lump of clay in the right hand,
one should go to pure water and perform the purification in the water.
In another tradition,
one should smear the penis with clay to the measure of an axle,
and likewise apply it everywhere, afterwards applying clay to the feet as well.
One should apply earth ten times to the left hand and seven times to both hands;
this is the specific rule in the *Suprabheda*: one application to the penis, five to the anus, and fifteen to the left hand.
Having joined the seven [fingers] of both hands together, one should then place the three [toes] on the feet and the buttocks.
One should always purify [the teeth] with water; this is prescribed for householders.
It has been stated that for students (brahmacārins), this [period of purification] is double that of householders.
And for those dwelling in the forest it is threefold, and for ascetics it is fourfold.
Furthermore, in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā:
"One should wash the anus and the penis with earth and pure water;
one should perform purification for the purpose of removing odor and stains—this is the established doctrine. (*) (**) [Note: The asterisks indicate the end of the citation.]
One should perform purification with as much earth as is necessary for the purity of the mind;
likewise,
one should fetch earth from a riverbank or from a mountain.
And at the root of an aśvattha tree, or even at a bilva tree or a thorny bush.

In a pure place such as a grove or similar location, the best of Brahmins should always avoid taking clay from these: from mud, from black earth, from a path, from saline soil, or from a wall; he should always shun these types of earth.

And the five types of clay that should not be taken are: that remaining after purification has been performed, clay from an anthill, clay from a saline wasteland, clay from within water, and clay from a temple.
One should not take earth from the banks of tanks or ponds for bathing, nor for excretion,
sexual intercourse, spitting, or brushing the teeth.
"Silence is prescribed during the six [occasions]: while eating and at the time of bathing. Thus it is said.
Having risen from that bank and honored [the deity], one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana);
then, having washed both feet and hands in the sequence beginning with the right.
He should perform all ritual actions with the right hand alone.
On dry land, he should place his right foot forward and his left foot in the water;
looking toward the sky and the directions, he should form his hands like the ears of a cow.
O child, having sipped water according to the rules and performed the ritual sprinkling with the mantra,
[one should do so] with the glorious five-syllabled mantra and then with the Śaiva Gāyatrī.
If one drinks water silently so that only a bean sinks within it,
having thus drunk three such draughts, one should not touch the mouth with the thumb.
Seated comfortably in a clean place, facing either the east or the north,
one should perform the cleansing of the teeth according to the rules after sipping water (ācamana) for the sake of purity.
Moist, containing fibers, of appropriate height, straight, clean, without joints,
and as wide as the little finger— such is recommended for cleaning the teeth.

The wood of the *nibimba*, *bilva*, *karañja*, *paukaṣa*, *khadira*, and *arjuna* should be eight finger-breadths long for those seeking liberation; now it is described for those seeking worldly enjoyment.
[One should avoid] those produced from the Plakṣa, Āmra, Kaśubha, Śoka, Jambū, and Campaka;
as well as the Audumbara, Apāmārga, Atimukta, Nimba,
Tintriṇī, Veṇu, Pruṣṭa, Kadamba, and Vadī.
Having taken for oneself [the clay] eight times, this [length] should be twelve finger-breadths;
or else, O Brahmin, among the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of the lowest castes.
It is prescribed as ten finger-breadths, decreasing by one finger-breadth at each step in sequence.
One should indeed take the *śarmadā*, *tridhā*, *daṇḍa*, *kṣīrī*, *kuṃbhyā*, and *kuśa* grasses;
[and] avoid the *śigru*, *vānīra*, *paiśāca*, *kāśa*, *aśvattha*, and *kuśa* [in this context].
In the Kāmika [Tantra]: Hintāla, tāla, kramuka, ketakī, and the great vaṭa,
along with nārikela and kharjūra— these seven are the "kings of grasses" (tṛṇarājikā).
O fair-faced one, by performing a bath with these pieces of wood grown from grass or trees,
a mortal shall truly fall into the state of a *caṇḍāla* on the first lunar day (*pratipad*),
on festival days, on the sixth, the twelfth, or the ninth day.
One should carefully avoid the contact of sticks with other sticks. On the day of a solar transit, on one's birthday, on the days of Vyatīpāta and Sunday,
and on the Nandā tithis as well as on festival days (parvan), one should avoid using a tooth-stick.
A wise person should personally perform the ritual with leaves, except on the new moon day and the eleventh lunar day.
And for those two as well, one should perform [the rite] with the tender leaves of the Plakṣa, Jambū, and Āmla trees.
But in the case of not obtaining a tooth-stick, [one may use] another [substance], except for a pebble.

The wise person should clean the teeth with the middle and ring fingers; alternatively, purification of the mouth may be achieved without brushing the teeth by performing twelve mouthfuls of gargling (gaṇḍūṣa), after which one should perform the ritual bath.
In another scripture, it is stated that bathing in the confluence of the Sindhu, in lakes, ponds, rivers, pools,
and even in natural springs, is exceedingly excellent.
In the case of lotus ponds and the like, the middle [measurement] is used;
furthermore, for small ponds, sacrificial pits, wells, and water reservoirs, bathing at home is the most excellent.
Furthermore, regarding the specific distinctions in the *Suprabheda*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme bath that removes sin;
five baths are prescribed for Brahmins, and through them they become pure."
Bathing is of five kinds: Vāruṇa, Āgneya, Divya, Vāyavya, and Mānasa.
Bathing with water is Vāruṇa; bathing with ashes is Āgneya.

The fivefold bath is declared as follows: the divine [bath] by means of rain accompanied by sunshine, the aerial by the dust of cows, and the mental by means of mantras. I shall now describe the Varuṇa, Āgneya, Divya, Vāyavya, and Mānasa baths.
And listen to it, O Gajānana!
Whether at a river, a pond, a lake, or even a well— of these four types—
if a well-bath is available, one should not perform it at ponds and the like.
O Gajānana, even when a river exists, one should not bathe in ponds; a large oblong pond is ten times more meritorious than a well, a true river is ten times more meritorious than a pond,
and a river flowing to the ocean is ten times more meritorious than that [ordinary] river.
The preceptor should proceed toward the east or the north for the purpose of bathing;
it is said that bathing while facing the east yields a hundredfold merit.
Even there, the southern bank is said to yield infinite fruit.
Whether the water be pure or impure, if it is in the vicinity of a temple of Śiva,
one should know it as the Śivagaṅgā, because of its service to the waters of Śiva’s abode.
Having approached their sacred ford, one should especially perform a bath;
this is declared to be the "bath for removing impurity. Now hear about the "mantra-bath" that follows.
Water inhabited by various aquatic creatures such as fish, frogs, and snakes is always frequented by living beings; therefore, it is especially impure.
To pacify those defects, however, one should prepare a sacred bathing place (śivatīrtha).
The practitioner should take pure clay, measuring one cubit in size and square on all four sides, while uttering the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*.
The mantrin should establish [the vessel] with *Sadyojāta*, sprinkle it with *Vāmadeva*,
touch it with *Aghora*, and divide it into three parts with *Puruṣa*;
he should then cast them toward the east, the south, and likewise the north.
One should consecrate each [portion] with the Īśāna mantra;
having recited the Astra, Brahma, and Śiva mantras, one should place them in order starting from the east.
Furthermore, the portion consecrated with the Astra mantra should be cast in the ten directions.
One should cast that portion which has been consecrated by the recitation of the Śiva-mantra into the midst of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
By means of the mantra ending with the syllable *phaṭ*, and through the application of various scriptural methods,
there shall be the eradication of those subtle defects that exist within the water.
One should sharpen one's own limbs with half of what remains from the *brahmajapta* [water],
[dividing it] part by part for the head, face, heart, feet,
and private parts; then, having touched oneself with the remaining half, one should bathe repeatedly with water.
Then, having touched water, one should bathe in the midst of the Śiva-tīrtha [if one has been defiled] by the appearance of deformities on the body arising from pigeons,
cocks, hawks, crows, herons, donkeys, dogs,
village pigs, vultures, or owls.
Upon touching a corpse fallen in a cremation ground, a ghost, a woman who has recently given birth, funeral garlands, food [from such sources],
or others bearing sectarian marks (liṅgin), one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
If there is contact with semen, feces, or urine above the navel— excluding the hands—
one should immerse oneself in water for purification after vomiting or shaving.
Bathing at night is not recommended, except during an eclipse;
for rivers constantly flow with blood at night.
Therefore, one should never perform bathing or drinking [of water] at night; however, one may indeed take it for the sake of the gods or for oneself.
Either in the presence of fire and gold, or with water,
the most excellent preceptor, having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), should cause [the disciple] to perform them.
Purification by water should be performed in this manner; one should go for a bath at night.
Therefore, one should indeed take a lamp for the sake of the deity and for oneself.
At the conclusion of the water-play, however, one should perform the consecration with facial mudrās.
Having performed the ritual bath with the limbs of Śiva-Brahman and the limbs of Vidyā, the wise practitioner [proceeds].
One should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times with the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva;
then, having established the sacred water (tīrtha) as being of the nature of Śiva by means of mantras whose essence is Śiva.
One should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) with the water from that [vessel] using the Saṃhitā mantras. One should join the water falling from the left hand with the right hand,
and perform the sprinkling on the head in sequence with those mantras using that water.

Having bowed, one should imagine white water in the form of the syllable *Boḍ* situated within the hollow of the right hand at the tip of its raised nose, and draw it in with the left [hand]. One should then release it.
One should cast the water from the *tattva* vessel, which contains the reflection of the lotus and the appearance of gain, along with the *piṅgā* and the *rīcha*,
onto a diamond-stone (*vajraśilā*) so that it may wash away the sins of the world;
while submerged in water, one should close the eyes and not sprinkle any part of the body at all.
And then one should show half [of it], with the face submerged from the belly;
that which is described as "face-submerged" (mukhamagna) shall, in sequence, be one hundred and fifty [units].
When half of a thousand has been submerged, it is called a *koṭi*;
one should thus perform this daily and then recite the Śiva-mantra.
Having emerged while absorbed in meditation, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in due order according to reality;
then, having touched ashes and water, he should gradually apply them to his head and other parts of the body.
The wise one should recite the Śiva-mantra according to his ability, accompanied by the Brahma-aṅgas;
then, with the mantra ending in *phaṭ*, he should collect the Śiva-tīrtha water.
One should take up a washed cloth and avoid one that is still wet.
Furthermore, in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā it is said:
"A man should bathe with a pure disposition, preceded by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa),
in a river, a pond, a well, a mountain spring, or a lake."
In a well, a skillful person, being composed, should bathe with water drawn out;
if unable, he may bathe up to the neck or even up to the waist.
Having sipped water (ācamana), one should put on a large garment and then sip water again.
If one is unable to perform the morning bath, one should perform the midday bath.
This has been declared as the water bath; now listen to the ash bath (bhasmasnāna).
Alternatively, in the Agnihotra rites, the wise one should take up the ashes;
for after [the ritual], the bath of ashes is prescribed even without a bath in water.
One should perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) after chanting the Śiva-Brahmāṅga mantra. Seated comfortably in a clean place, pure in heart and purified,
one should perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) while facing either the east or the north.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme rite of bathing with ashes,
which brings fortune, is purifying, and serves as a necklace and an ornament.
Then, having taken the sacred ash with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*), having placed it on the palm of the left hand, and having covered it with the right hand,

one should consecrate it six times with the *praṇava* and the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarī*). Then, having smeared the sacred ash (*vibhūti*) on the head with the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām," one should smear the face with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra, and smear the heart with the *aghora* mantra.

Having smeared the navel with the Vāmadeva mantra, having smeared the feet with the Sadyojāta mantra, and having performed the dusting of all limbs with the *praṇava* (Oṃ), one should take up the sacred ash with the mantra "Mā nastoke," apply water with "Śaṃ no devīḥ," and stir it with "Mā no mahāntam. In the center of that, [one should draw] a five-cornered [figure].

Having drawn [the diagram] starting from the east, having written the letters beginning with *na* and ending with *ya* in the five corners, and having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the center, one should consecrate it eight times with the five-syllabled *praṇava* mantra; immediately thereafter, one should apply the sacred ash (*vibhūti*) to each limb.
It is as follows:
The wise man, having remembered Śiva on his head, should apply the sacred ash;
he should remember Māheśvara on his forehead and Rudra on both ears.
One should worship Śrīkaṇṭha on the throat, Śambhu on the pair of arms, Īśvara on the region of the heart,
and Mahādeva on the navel and the back.
On the shoulder [the wise one] should apply Paśupati, then Śaṅkara on the pair of arms;
Vṛṣadhvaja on the region of the hump, and likewise Paramātman on both wrists— thus should the wise man wear the sacred ash (vibhūti).
Thus, having assumed his majestic power.
The production of ashes is taught by those who know the tantras as being fourfold:
the primary ritual (kalpa), the secondary ritual (anukalpa), the subsidiary ritual (upakalpa), and the ritual-less (akalpaka).
Taking a single ladleful of water into vessels such as jars and the like,
one should perform the ritual bath at the three junctions of the day, or as often as possible.
At the time of bathing, having washed his hands and feet with pure water, he should,
remaining silent, consecrate the ashes eight times with the root mantra.
One should sprinkle the head with the Īśāna mantra, the face likewise with the Puruṣa mantra,
the region of the heart with the Aghora mantra, the private parts with the Vāmadeva mantra,
the feet with the Sadyojāta mantra, and all the limbs with the Praṇava itself.
This is the supreme fire-based bath (āgneya-snāna) performed with ashes;
having consecrated the ashes eight times with the root mantra,
one should smear the body with them and also wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra).
Moreover, the smearing of all limbs with ashes is not equal to the triple marks (tripuṇḍra);
therefore, one should apply only the triple mark, even without the smearing.
The best of practitioners should always wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on fifteen places of the body with ashes mixed with water.
On the head, on the forehead, and likewise on the two ears;
on the neck, on the two arms, on the heart, on the navel, and on the back.
One should wear the *tripuṇḍra* mark with ashes on both arms, on the shoulder region, and likewise on the two wrists, either with the root mantra or otherwise.
Using only the three middle fingers of one's own right hand,
one should apply the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead with a measurement of six finger-breadths, or even more, according to the measure of one's two eyes.
One should apply the *puṇḍra* with the middle, ring, and thumb fingers, either in the forward or reverse order; thus it becomes "with Rudra," of this there is no doubt.
Advancing white, wide-spread, smooth, and measuring the width of the ear—
this Tripuṇḍra, endowed with these auspicious characteristics, bestows all spiritual perfections.
Immediately following that, the procedure for sipping water (*ācamana*) is described:

**Ūṃ raṇiraṇiśvatomaśmaṃ (namaḥ śaṃ-) bhave ca mayo bhave ca namaḥ śaṃkarāya ca.** With these three mantras, one should perform the sipping of water. With the tips of all the fingers [one says] *mayaskarāya ca*. On the upper lip, **ūṃ namaḥ**.

One should touch the lower lip with the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," and the chin with "Oṃ namaḥ śivatarāya. With the thumb and forefinger, one should touch the left nostril with "Oṃ bhavodbhavāya namaḥ," and the right eye with "Jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ" using the thumb and ring finger. One should touch the right eye with "Śreṣṭhāya namaḥ."
Salutation to Rudra on the left eye; salutation to Kāla on the right ear;
salutation to Kalavikaraṇa with the little finger and thumb on the left ear; salutation to Balavikaraṇa with the palm at the navel.
One should touch the belly. One should touch the four limbs with the tips of the fingers, as follows: salutation to Bala with the tips of the fingers on the head.

Salutation to Balapramathana; on the right arm: *ūṃ*, salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana; on the left arm: salutation to Manonmana. On the chest, with the palm of the left hand [touching] the palm of the right hand: "Salutation be to you, O Blessed One, Lord of the Universe (*Viśveśvara*); salutation to Mahādeva. With the palm of the right hand [touching] the palm of the left hand: salutation to Mahādeva.

One should touch the eight limbs with the palm of the right hand as follows: "Salutation to Tryambaka" on the sole of the right foot; "Salutation to Trikālāgni" on the left foot; "Salutation to Kālāgnirudra" on the right side; "Salutation to Nīlakaṇṭha" on the left side; "Salutation to Sarveśvara" on the chest; "Salutation to Śrī Mahādeva" on the right neck; and one should touch the head. Thus it has been said.
In the Vāmadevasaṃhitā, there are six mantras beginning with "namaḥ śambhave" which constitute the *manavas*.
"Bhavodbhavāya ī namaḥ"—this is known as the first *namaḥ*.

Eleven mantras are recorded as belonging to Vāmadeva. They are remembered as follows: "Oṃ, salutation to you, O Blessed One, Lord of the Universe"; "Mahādeva"; "Tryambaka"; "Tripurāntaka"; "Trinayana"; "Agnikāla"; "Kālāgnirudra";
"Nīlakaṇṭha"; "Sarveśvara"; and "Sadāśiva. These, beginning with "Śrīmahādeva," are recorded as being joined with the word "salutation" (*namaḥ*).
Twenty-eight great names have been proclaimed; the wise say that acts such as sipping water (ācamana) and so forth should be performed with these.
Having drunk [the water] with the three mantras beginning with Śambhu, one should touch [the body] with the remaining [mantras];
then, immediately thereafter, one should touch the two lips and the chin with the tips of the fingers.
One should touch the twelve limbs with the mantras beginning with *bhavodbhava*.
One should touch the two nostrils in sequence with the thumb and forefinger;
one should touch the eyes and ears in sequence with the thumb and ring finger.
One should touch the navel and the abdomen with the little finger and the thumb together,
the head with the tips of the fingers, and the armpits with the base of the fingers.
One should touch the ten limbs with the mantras beginning with "namaste";
specifically, one should touch the right palm with the very surface of the left hand.
Likewise, with the right hand one should touch the palm of the left hand,
the two feet, the two sides, the chest, and both cheeks.
O tiger among sages, [this] occurs by the very palm of the head-lord, and not otherwise.
"Having thus sipped water according to the rule, one should perform the ritual acts.
Now, the procedure for the *saṃdhyā* is described:
with all the fingers joined together, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) preceded by inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*).

And likewise Āpastamba says: "Or desiring to accomplish half [the goal]. Regarding this, the Commentator (*vṛttikāra*) states: "Desiring to accomplish—that is, wishing to achieve—an object (*artha*), whether visible or invisible, one should practice breath-restraint (*prāṇāyāma*) until exhaustion, that is, until the fatigue of the body occurs. One should perform three rounds of breath-restraint," as stated in the *Śāradātilaka*.
Having first performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the Gāyatrī at the two junctions of the day (saṃdhyā).
The best of practitioners, reciting three times the Gāyatrī together with the seven vyāhṛtis and accompanied by the Śiras, should restrain the vital breaths (prāṇas) with focused concentration.
This is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*, the remover of all sins.

The meaning is that *prāṇāyāma* is defined as the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consisting of the threefold recitation of the *gāyatrī* mantra, preceded by the seven *vyāhṛtis* together with the syllable *oṃ*, and accompanied by the *śiras* mantra "Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ. [The first stage is] *pūraka*.

The practices of *kumbhaka* and *recaka* are shown in other texts: "Inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*) constitute the threefold characteristic of *prāṇāyāma*. Drawing [the breath] in through the nose and filling it within is called *pūraka*."
Kumbhaka is the breath that is still; recaka is that which is being emptied.
Regarding the question of how these are to be performed, Vāmadeva says:
"Seated properly upon a seat, having filled the abdomen with the left [nostril]..."
"By means of retention (*kumbhaka*), having performed the cycle three times, one should exhale through the right [nostril].
Regarding the performance of *prāṇāyāma*, he states the specific rule for householders and others:
"The pressing of the tip of the nose with five fingers is called the *praṇava* seal; this destroys all sins."
For the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*), the pressing of the tip of the nose with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb is prescribed.
For the ascetic (*yati*) and the student (*brahmacārin*), it is called the *Oṃkāra-mudrā*. One should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) while keeping the eyes closed.
And the mantra is: *Oṃ bhūḥ; Oṃ bhuvaḥ; Oṃ svaḥ; Oṃ mahaḥ; Oṃ janaḥ.*

*Ūṃ tapaḥ*. *Ūṃ gū satyam*. *Ūṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*. *Ūṃ āpo jyotiraso'mṛtaṃ brahma bhūrbhuvaḥ suvar om*. The meaning of this is as follows: Here, first is the word *praṇava*, *ūṃ*. *Bhūḥ*: the Rudra deities presiding over the earthly realm (*bhūrloka*). Those thousands upon thousands of Rudras—

"Regarding the phrase *adhibhūmyām*, according to the scripture, those who are praised as being Brahman—namely Śiva, whose name signifies Consciousness (*cidākāra*) and who is the meaning of the syllable *Oṃ*—are indicated by this intended sense (*tātparya*).

As it is stated in the *Mahopaniṣad*: 'The sound which is proclaimed at the beginning of the Vedas and established at the end of the Vedas—that which is higher than that [sound] when it has dissolved into its source is Maheśvara. Furthermore, the Rudra-deities presiding over the *bhūrloka* [have been described] by me..."

With the intention of requesting permission for the daily rites (*āhnika*) to have been completed, he first describes that word (*tat-pada*) in order to offer his performed actions to the respective Rudra-deities with devotion and faith; therein follows the method for the derivation of the form *om*.
From the verbal root *ava* (or *ava*), meaning "to protect" (*rakṣaṇa*), by applying the suffix *manin* according to the *Uṇādi-sūtra* "avateṣṭilopaśca," and upon the elision of the *ṭi*-portion...

When "api amī" is established, the substitution *ūṭh* is applied by the rule *jvaratvaretyādinā*. When the vowel *u* is reached for the letter *v*, the *guṇa* substitution is applied by the rule *ādguṇaḥ*. Upon the pronunciation of the remaining portion, the form *ūm* is produced—consisting of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*. According to the scripture, "May that [which consists of] the letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m* become one; that indeed is *oṃ*. Thus, the word *ūṃkāra* has the meaning of Brahman. (Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary sentence at the end regarding the meaning of the term *ūṃkāra* as Brahman.)

The etymological derivation is: "He protects" (*vati rakṣati*) or "He causes one to cross over the ocean of saṃsāra. *Ūṃ* refers to the deities of the sky and rivers presiding over the *bhūrloka*. *Ūṃ* signifies those whose nature is consciousness, who are identical with Śiva and Brahman. According to the Śruti, "Those born in this great ocean, in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)," [it refers to] the Rudra-deities who are the lords of the upper regions and reside in the worlds such as *bhuvarloka* and above.
Because they exist, this should be understood to apply likewise for Bhuvarloka and the other worlds. It is stated in the Śivadharmaśāstra:
"O gods who dwell in Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, and Svarloka, endowed with divine splendor, may you always grant me peace."
Those gods who dwell in Maharloka, Janaloka, and the worlds of Tapas and Satya—
those joyful deities, possessing the luster of refined gold— [also rejoice].

"May they, eternally bowed to as Īśāna, always grant me peace"—in this [mantra], the words *mahas*, *janas*, *tapaḥ*, and *sat* end in the suffix *-asun*. It should be understood that the recitation of the *praṇava* (Oṃ) at every step is for the sake of firmness. The identity of the Rudra-deities residing in the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ is with Śiva alone, either by way of being his body (*śarīrabhāvena*) or by way of being his aspect (*vibhāvena*).

Or rather, it is appropriate because its existence (*sattā*) is non-different from that [of the deity]; thus, it is another deity. As for *gāyatrī*, however, it will be explained at the occasion of the recitation (*japa*).
It should be understood as "Oṃ, the waters, light—this is the head of the *gāyatrī*. Its meaning is as follows: Oṃ, the waters (*āpaḥ*) are those who have become Brahman, designated as Paraśiva.

The plural number is used because of the lexicographical rule (*kośa*) stating "the word *āpas* denotes the feminine gender in the plural. Light (*jyotis*) is the splendor (*tejas*) shining in the sky. Oṃ, [it refers to] the one designated as Paramaśiva.

It is stated that Rudra—who, according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), is "he who has become Brahman, who is in the fire, who is in the waters," and so forth—is the Lord whose body consists of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*) as the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). As stated in the *Śaivasiddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*: "The phenomenal world, from earth up to the Self, exists in an eightfold manner."
This self of the Lord is his subtle body, the controller of all principles;
it is superior to that manifest world which has become the body of the Supreme Being.
For the God who has become the self, there is neither division nor separate existence.

*Rasa* refers to mercury (*pārada*). "Ūṃ, O you who are named Paramaśiva, you who have become Brahman"—this is stated because Śiva, the primordial physician, is of the nature of *rasa*, according to the Vedic scripture: "I hear that You are the best of physicians among physicians. And it is said therein: "The primordial physician Maheśvara exists there as the essence of *rasa*. Alternatively, *ūṃ* signifies the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda; for the lexicon states: "Brahman is austerity (*tapas*). Thus: "Ūṃ, O you who are named Paramaśiva, you who have become Brahman."

From the scripture, "I am devoid of essence among the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan [Vedas]," it is understood that the terms *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *suvaḥ* are indicative of the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ. These are the worlds starting with Bhūḥ. *Oṃ*, you are the Supreme Śiva, the one who has become Brahman; he who is Rudra is indeed the Blessed Lord. To him who is *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *suvah*, salutations again and again. You are the head, the giver of people (*janada*), and the form of Virañci (Brahmā). He who is indeed...

Rudra is that Blessed One who is Bhūḥ; salutations again and again to him who is Bhūr-bhuvaḥ. Rudra is that Blessed One who is Suvaḥ; Rudra is that Blessed One who is Mahaḥ; Rudra is that Blessed One who is Janaḥ; Rudra is that Blessed One who is Tapaḥ; Rudra is that Blessed One who is Satyaḥ. To him who is Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ—[salutations].

"Indeed, salutation after salutation! The head is 'janada om viśvam āpo nīti' according to the Śruti. Since it is prescribed that one who desires to accomplish a purpose [should perform breath control], the distinction is that breath control (prāṇāyāma) comes first, and thereafter the formal resolve (saṅkalpa).

Having thus performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord, I shall perform the morning twilight ritual (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*)," one should take auspicious water in another vessel with the left hand. It has been stated in another treatise which vessel should be used for the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*). [End of quote].
At the bank of a river or a pond, or in a vessel made of clay,
or one made of udumbara wood, or of gold, silver, or stone.

"Or, holding [the vessel] in the left hand, one should perform the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsti*). Thus [it is said]. Since it is stated that "audumbara" means copper—that is, *audumbara* is copper, and *śruva* is [made of] copper—one should recite: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ; Oṃ, we meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects. By means of this [mantra] known as the "mouth of Brahmā."
Having consecrated that water with the mantra—*ūṃ hāṃ*, this being the mantra called "the Mouth"—it is stated in another text (*granthāntara*):
"The syllable *ūṃ*, the first three great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), and the three-footed *gāyatrī* should be known as the 'Mouth of Brahman'"; thus, it is the *gāyatrī* together with the *śiras*.

It is stated elsewhere that [the mouth] is the "mouth of Brahman. Having touched that [water], one should perform the sprinkling (*mārjana*) with water consecrated by the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and others, using *darbha* grass, over the head—that is, with the "head of the Gāyatrī," beginning with "oṃ āpaḥ" and so forth; this is the meaning of "with the head. "Consecrated" (*abhiṣṭutam*) means "empowered by mantras" (*abhimantraṇa*). He states a specific detail regarding the sprinkling:
One should perform the purification (mārjana) with water from kuśa grass using the verses together with the syllable Om (praṇava) for each quarter-verse;
then, one should cast water along with kuśa grass while reciting "yasya kṣayāya. Thus it is said.

He states the number of the *mārjana* verses: "The group of nine beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, both [verses] beginning with *dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam*, the four [verses] beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and the four *varṇāḥ*—they know [these] as twenty-four. Thus it is said.

It has been stated that the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) should be performed with the *devatīrtha* [finger-position]. One should perform the acts of sprinkling, worship, offering oblations (*balikarman*), and eating with the *devatīrtha*. The mantras prescribed for the sprinkling are written here: "O Waters, you who are most refreshing; grant us strength for great joy and for clear vision. Grant us a share of that most auspicious essence of yours, like longing mothers. From that...
Do not be angry; for the sake of whose prosperity you quicken, O Waters, bring forth progeny. The meaning of this [verse] beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" is as follows:

O Waters—referring to the deities presiding over the water, namely the Rudras—the word *hi* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*; thus, the sense culminates in "you alone. "Mayobhuvaḥ": having abandoned the cruelty mentioned in the mantra regarding how [beings] pierce those drinking from vessels, [look upon us] with a gracious gaze.
"O waters, you are easy to obtain for drinking, bathing, and other uses; you are manifold. The lengthening of the vowel is Vedic.

You are eleven in number, according to the Śruti: 'You are eleven by greatness. The word *maya* signifies happiness, for the Śruti says: 'That which is happiness (or auspiciousness, *śiva*) is indeed *maya*';
and also because of the etymological interpretation: 'For you, O waters, are indeed happiness (*sukha-bhuvah*'). Furthermore, you have Rudra as your deity. Thus, you are composed of happiness."

"Establish us in *ūrj* (sustenance) through your grace"—for the etymological interpretation (*nirukti*) shows that *ūrj* means food (*anna*). According to the *Śruti*, "It is the sustainer of Aila. O Sun, having increased my own heroic power and other qualities—which reside in the state of the clouds—by means of the falling showers, and having provided for us abundance such as grain and the like; [may you do so].

The intended meaning is: "Establish us as those worthy of receiving your grace. Furthermore, regarding *mahe*: for the sake of the great (*mahate*), for the sake of sport (*raṇāya*), and for the sake of seeing (*cakṣase*). There is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the knowledge of the thumb (*tarjanya-jñāne*). Thus, the connection with the preceding verse is: "Grant [us] that which is conducive to the knowledge of oneness with Śiva (*śivaikya-jñāna*). Therefore, it means: "Make us possessed of the yoga of the knowledge of oneness with Śiva. *Namaḥ*.

According to the Vedic revelation, "there is great fear," the deity Rudra has now requested food preceded by the prefix *vi-* (i.e., spoiled or putrid food), and his abode is being described as harsh with power. "By your water" (*yonāvaḥ*): that which is situated in your abode, the water, is most auspicious (*śivatama*) and exceedingly pleasant because it exists within your domain. That which is tasted or relished is called *rasa*; here, it refers to a specific kind of flavor.

"Naḥ" means "us"; it should be understood that the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative to denote "that [stream] of His," as a grace. "Bhājayata" means "cause us to attain," for the Śruti says, "And the essence is mine. If one asks how, the meaning is: "uśatīḥ" means "desiring" or "endowed with affection.
The second person plural is used in the sense of the first person plural by Vedic license (chāndasam), with the ellipsis "mothers [attain] their own sons. Just as...
Just as mothers, being affectionate toward their offspring, cause their own calves to drink from their milk, so too you—the deities presiding over the waters—are affectionate toward your devotees;

the sense is that you should cause those situated in your devotion to partake of the essence of your grace. "We take up *tejas*" means for the sake of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Now, he requests another kind of essence residing in that presiding deity, beginning with the words "of whom" (*yasya*). Of whom... [text continues]

"For the depletion of rasa" means for its dwelling; the use of the dative case in the sense of the instrumental is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. "Jinvatha" means you become pleased. The meaning is: depending upon what specific kind of *rasa* you become immersed in supreme bliss, we, for the sake of attaining such grace from you, would go (*gamāma*)—that is, we would go intensely (*aram*)—unto you.
O Adhiṣṭhānendra deities, whatever specific excellence of flavor exists in your abode,
grant that specific excellence of flavor to us as a favor; thus [says] Adhiṣṭha...
The intended meaning is that the deities presided over by Rudra are being invoked. The underlying thought is: "We take up vigor for the sake of virility. Furthermore:

"The fathers placed the embryo, the youth adorned with a lotus-garland; may a man here sit [in prosperity]. Having heard this, since it is observed that the attainment of a son results from the consumption of the *piṇḍa* (funeral cake) from the middle of the hands during the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* performed for the deities presided over by Rudra, he [performs] it for that purpose.

The deities of Rudra are invoked in the morning with the mantra "O Waters. O Waters, you who have Rudra as your presiding deity, do not produce those who are afflicted by heat; rather, bestow upon us that specific essence of grace and bring about for us the prosperity of sons who are devotees of Śiva. The sense is: "We accept [you] for the sake of nourishment and procreation. Having thus performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*), [one proceeds].

Immediately after that, one should perform the drinking of water. The mantra for the drinking of water is written as follows: "May Sūrya and Manyu, and the lords of wrath, protect me from the sinful deeds committed out of wrath. Whatever sin I have committed during the night—with my mind, with my speech, with my two hands, with my feet, with my belly, or with my genitals—may the Night wipe it away. And whatever misfortune is in me."
"Here I offer myself into the sun, the light whose source is immortality; Svāhā! The meaning of this is as follows: "Sūrya" refers to Rudra, the soul of the sun;

"Manyu" is his anger; and the meaning is that the power (*śakti*) is of the nature of that anger. "O Lords of Manyu" refers to the masters, and the hosts of Rudras who have become his rays and are his attendants.

"Yellow, copper-colored, ruddy, and even tawny, most auspicious are they"—for it is heard in scripture: "Those Rudras who are stationed by the thousands in every direction, may they all [protect] us. From all those sins and misfortunes committed through *manyu*—that is, through anger—[may they protect us].

"May they protect me! May they not [harm] me!"—the *loṭ* suffix is used here in the sense of a prayer. The meaning is: "May all the gods protect me, a devotee of Śiva, by destroying that sin. Furthermore, "whatever [sin] night after night"—the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the seventh (*saptamī*), according to the rule *pariṇatyuta*;
the sense is that [the sin consists of] the mental failure to contemplate the Lord and the vocal failure to utter the names and hymns of Śiva.

[The form] "hastābhyām" [expresses] the nature of performing the worship of Śiva with the two hands; "padbhyām" [expresses] the nature of going to the sacred sites of Śiva and so forth with the two feet; "udareṇa" [expresses] the nature of eating desired food with the belly; "śiśnā" [expresses] the nature of engaging in sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached with the penis. Some desire the suffix *kvip* [here]; others say it is a Vedic form. [The thought is: "I have committed a sin."

The connection applies everywhere. That [sin], however, is of such a nature: night is the power (*śakti*) in the form of night, inherent in Śiva and the beloved of the Trident-bearer (*śūlapāṇi*), according to the statement "She is *hī*. May she take it away; that is, may she remove it. And as for whatever other sin—consisting of the absence of knowledge of union with Śiva—that has been produced in me, both this misfortune and its perpetrator, myself: [may she remove them].

I [am established] in the immortal source—the immortal Brahman which is the cause of liberation, according to the Śruti: "In the immortal Brahman. In the Sun—that is, in the solar orb existing within the heart-lotus and consisting of the Sun—according to the Śruti: "He is established in the twelve-spoked wheel. In the Light—that is, in the self-luminous—according to [the Śruti]: "The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Him alone..."

"Everything shines after Him; by His light all this is illumined"—so says the Śruti. "I offer, that is, I cast, [all] into the Supreme Śiva who resides within my own self. For the Śruti declares: "He who is here in the person and He who is yonder in the sun, He is one. By means of this oblation, I [offer] all that.

The meaning is "I reduce to ashes. *Svāhā* means "let there be a well-offered oblation. This is the mantra for consuming water at midday: *Āpaḥ punantu*. Regarding the waters: they have Agni as their presiding deity and Rudra as their divinity, according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) which states, "The waters have Agni as their lord; they are impelled by the waters; they are great, eleven-fold. By the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*), [one refers to] the earth.

My gross physical body composed of earth is perceived; they call the gross [body] "earthy. It consists of the five elements and is devoid of pride. According to the *Yogadīpikā*, it is composed of the network of principles (*tattva*) beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas.
May they purify—that is, make holy—my gross physical body composed of earth. May they cause my gross body to be purified; [thus] my body becomes pure. Its own desired [state is attained].

Purified by the hosts of Rudras; O Earth, according to the Vedic revelation that "there are eleven [Rudras] stationed in the midst," may they purify—that is, cleanse—me, the individual soul (jīvātman), who am devoted to Me, along with the hosts of Rudras. According to the two Vedic passages beginning with "Those who are tawny among the trees, blue-necked and bright red," they reside in the supreme tree, or rather, in all living beings, both stationary and moving, such as trees, possessing blue necks and so forth.

Specifically, Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara has explained that "there are Rudras" refers to those who are distinguished; the meaning is: "May [He] make me fit for the worship of Śiva mentioned hereafter. *Brahmaṇaspati*: the Lord (*pati*) of *brahman*—that is, of the syllable *oṃ* which is dissolved in *prakṛti*—is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). He who is declared the primordial sound at the beginning of the Vedas and is established at the end of the Vedas, of Him who is dissolved in *prakṛti*...

"He who is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) of another," according to the Śruti. May the Brahman—that is, the syllable *oṃ* which denotes it—purify us. "Brahman" refers to the syllable *oṃ*; this is an indication of the non-difference between the signified and the signifier. "Pūtā" [is used for] "pūtam"; the very long vowel is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). "May it purify me"—may it effect my oneness with Śiva, that is, union (*sāyujya*), according to the Śruti regarding its application (*viniyoga*).

One should not eat what is left over or what has been offered to other deities. In the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā it is said: "Even in times of extreme distress, a man should not, even through negligence, eat what has been offered to other deities; he would cut out his own tongue. Thus, [he should exclude] outsiders along with their servants and so forth.
Regarding that which was uttered there: "The Rākṣasas, performers of cruel deeds, endowed with sinful conduct, will prevail in the Kali age; those men who are revilers shall be cast out.
Those who have previously committed the murder of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, or the theft of gold shall become outcasts."
"Those who revile the Lord of the Kali age—one should not speak with them, nor sit with them, nor share a seat with them;

one should not eat in their company, nor form kinship with them. Thus [it is said]. All this [I offer], as well as the acceptance of gifts from the wicked who are devoid of devotion to Śiva, and water—O Rudra-gaṇas, may you purify me! I offer this into the Kālāgnirudra fire, which is established upon the root of my own self.

In the *Bṛhajjābālopaniṣad*: "This Kālāgni is bound by Ādhāraśakti and moves upward above the spokes of the wheel. *Svāhā* means "may it be well offered"; the meaning is that it reduces everything to ashes. The mantra for the consumption of water at evening is *agniśca*.
Agni is Rudra, the one who moves through the limbs (*aṅgātiga*). Indeed, this Agni is Rudra; furthermore, he is the wrath of Rudra himself.

The meaning is that the power (śakti) has anger as its essence. And the lords of wrath (manyupatayaḥ) are the masters of anger, whose forms are sparks of the nature of anger. These hosts of Rudras—may they all protect me from the misfortunes (duritāni) created by wrath, that is, produced by the impulse of anger; this is an imperative (loṭ) used in the sense of a prayer. May all the gods [protect] me, a devotee of Śiva, through the consumption of wind and other elements.
The meaning is "may he protect. Furthermore, regarding the word *ahna*: it occurs in the locative case (*ahni*), the intended sense being that the third case is transformed into the seventh.

[One should protect] by means of the mind in the form of contemplating the Lord; by means of speech in the form of reciting hymns of praise to the names of Śiva; by means of the two hands in the form of performing the worship of Śiva; by means of the two feet in the form of going to the sacred sites (*kṣetra*) of Śiva; and by means of the belly...

[The form] consisting of the performance of eating offered to the lords by means of the belly; here, by the word *jaṭhara*, the organ of excretion (*pāyurindriya*) is meant. [The form] consisting of the performance of approaching those who should not be approached by means of the penis (*śiśna*); some desire the suffix *kvip* [here].
By the phrase "this is a Vedic form," the connection is made with "I have committed sin" in every instance. This form—that is, this sin—I have [committed] today.

Śiva is the day, the form of light, as stated in the scripture: "The god is the one who holds the trident. May he "avalumpatu"—that is, may he remove or protect [me] from. Regarding the phrase "yatkiñca" (whatever):

whatever sin in the form of moving away from the meditation on Śiva, or whatever other evil has been produced within me; this misfortune, both the perpetrator and myself—[may he place us] in the "ahari," the source of immortality, which is the cause of liberation, according to the Vedic revelation: "Amṛta is Brahman. In the "satye," that which is free from sublation; in the Mūlādhāra.
I offer [myself] into the self-luminous light, which is of the nature of fire abiding within the circle of fire, existing as my own self, the supreme Śiva.

By this oblation, I mean that I reduce everything to ashes. He states the mantras for purification (*mārjana*): "O Dadhikrāvin... Dadhi is the oblation in the form of the universe; *krāmati* means it moves or pervades, thus *dadhikrā* is Rudra, whose essence is fire and who consumes all. Likewise, he is one...

Viṣṇu, the Great Being, the Soul of all beings, having pervaded the three worlds as manifold individual entities, enjoys them as the imperishable consumer of the universe. "Omnipresent, for the great devouring, for Maheśvara, and for Camasī," says Jābāli. "Ki" means "what? Regarding him, the one who has drunk the curd (*dadhikrāvī*), the victorious, the one whose nature is conquest, the pervasive horse—[this refers to] the attainment of the needle; he possesses *vāja*, which is food.

"Food belongs to the Victorious One (Vādin)," according to the Śruti; that is to say, because He alone is the eater of food for all the gods, the meaning is "of Him who is richly endowed with food," as per the Śruti: "Obeisance to the Lord of foods. Thus, I have performed [this rite] for Rudra, whose nature is Agni, because my sinful speech has come to rest.

According to the Vedic revelation, "Agni has indeed resorted to speech," the meaning is: "By means of speech, may I perform his hymn of praise; may I become his servant. And that Rudra, whose essence is Agni, is our mouths, as is seen in such passages as "He who has four horns. [The word] *surabhiṇaḥ* [is used] in the sense of *surabhiṇaḥ*. According to the Vedic revelation, "The gods are indeed water," [this refers to] all [the offerings] of that Rudra, whose essence is Agni.

May the gods, by consuming that [oblation] with favor, make us fragrant. Furthermore, may they cause our lifespan (*āyus*) to cross over—that is, to increase. This is the connection with the verbal root *tṛ* (to cross) used in the sense of "bestowing. Thus, may they cause our life-span, as proclaimed in the Veda, to flourish pre-eminently and without affliction; the sense is: "may they bestow grace upon us. At the end of the mantra:

The ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) should be performed; this is because it is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). [The first mantra is] "āpo hi ṣṭhā. Regarding the sprinkling, he states another mantra: "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ. [The waters] are golden-colored, beautiful as gold, pure, stainless, and purifying—all that sanctifies all living beings.
Such are the waters in which the desired deity Rudra resides. Furthermore, in those waters... [he resides].

Among the deities of Rudra, Kaśyapa is the beholder; Rudra is the soul of the Sun. The Vedic [form] is a permutation of the initial and final letters. "He who is copper-colored" is the Śruti. Born as Indra, Rudra is the Lord of the Sun, according to the Śruti: "Salutation to the blue-throated one, the thousand-eyed one. And he is born among the waters, among the desired deities. Virūpās are those of various forms, such as Nagna, Muṇḍa, and so forth. Salutation...

According to the Vedic revelation, "To the Virūpas," the waters have Agni as their presiding deity, along with the host of Rudras. Having dissolved into the fire—the fire of time (kālāgni)—they remain as a germ (*garbha*) held in the hand during the occasion of the dance (*nāṭya*). This is based on the lexicon which states: "The word *garbha* refers to an embryo and to the juncture of a dramatic performance. Some maintain that in the *Āgamas*, those waters are the waves (*velanāḥ*) of the dissolving fire. Thus, the waters, having Agni and the Rudra deities as their lords, are the causes of our well-being (*śam*) and happiness. They are our protectors.
The *Avaiṣika* [mantra] and the *Suśchanakāśca* [mantra], and also the *Caṃtu*. Regarding the *Mārjana* [mantra], he speaks another mantra not specifically enjoined:

"Of whom the King... Here, *taruṇa* refers to Rudra whose essence is Varuṇa, according to the Śruti: "O most bountiful one" (*mīḍhuṣṭama*). "King" (*rājā*) means the Lord (*prabhu*), that is to say, the independent one (*svatantra*). He is the one who, discerning truth and falsehood, merit and demerit among people, distributes them. Of whom... [the King].

Among those whose deity is Rudra who has not yet been propitiated, "in the forest" is the understood remainder. He goes—that is, he proceeds—to Rudra, [thinking] "this one is a doer of merit, this one is a doer of evil";

the meaning is that he dwells there with the desire to perform actions in the form of grace or punishment according to merit and evil. Moreover, from him flow streams of honey-like water in the form of favor; the purifiers (pāvakāḥ) abide there.

"La" and so forth. The rest has been explained. Regarding the phrase "of whom the gods": among those waters whose deities are Agni, Rudra, and others, certain groups of Rudra-gods—the gods—perform the drinking (*pratibhakṣa*) of those waters unseen in the heavenly world (*div*, *dyuloka*); certain groups of Rudra-gods drink them in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); and by means of the wind (*pravāyu*), [they drink] among humans, because of the presence of diseases, afflictions, and the like.

The afflictors of suffering are manifold and of various kinds. Those waters in the rivers which have Rudra as their deity, and those on the earth—those who pierce through foods and vessels while people drink; by the Vedic text "payā pāpayaḥ," they bind people with drink and moisten them. "Homage to the Rudras who are upon the earth; may they protect us with that," so says the Śruti. They are bright and radiant.

"Those waters"—the rest has been explained. Regarding "with the auspicious": O Waters, whose deity is Rudra, look upon me with an auspicious eye—that is, with an eye that is the very nature of Śiva—according to the statement of Vātūla: "O Gaṅgā, [look upon] the Śiva-liṅga. Look at me; cast upon me a continuous and abundant glance of compassion.

The meaning is "he accomplishes. [He prays: "May your auspicious body, O Śiva, touch my skin," according to the Vedic scripture: "O Rudra, that auspicious body of yours which you gaze upon. The meaning is: "By means of touching my skin, make it completely purified. Regarding the word "all": "O Waters, you who have Rudra as your deity, [I approach] you in the waters."
"They sink" and "they stand"—these are like words for water. Regarding the question, "In what manner does one offer to all the fires?", he says:

"O good refuge, bestow upon me luster (*varcas*), strength (*bala*), power (*śakti*), vigor (*ojas*), and enthusiasm (*utsāha*)—place all of this within me, establish it there. And make me possessed of luster, possessed of strength, and possessed of vigor. This is the meaning. From the verse beginning with *drupadāt*: "May [Rudra] release me from sin. Rudra is the witness of action, whose self is the Sun.

The remainder [is as follows]. In this regard, there is an illustration: "like a wooden foot-stake" (*drupada*). A wooden foot-stake (*drupada*) is a piece of wood fixed into the foot of an offender (*aparādhin*). It is well known that village headmen establish such wooden stakes, fixed to the feet, in the middle of a village in order to restrain thieves. The meaning is "just like that. For example, a compassionate master [releases someone] from bondage.

The meaning is that it releases the offender in the same manner. Furthermore: "May the waters cleanse (*śundhantu*), i.e., purify me from sin (*enas*). To this effect, three similes are stated: "From the wooden block (*drupadāt*)," and so forth. Just as one who is releasing pieces of wood and the like is released, [the word *mumucāna* is used]; likewise, [the forms] *svinnaḥ*, *snātvī*, and *snātvyādi* are formed with the suffix *niṣṭhā* (kta), which is prescribed after the root *snā*. Thus, the form *apsu* is correct.

"May the non-malicious [waters] touch me, pervading even from the mud. With this verse ending in "purifies by means of this," one should prepare two tips of *darbha* grass as *pavitra*—that is, as a purifier—measuring a span (*prādeśa*) and having tips, as seen in the Śrauta tradition:
"The *pavitra* is indeed the two *darbha* blades."

This is because of the Vedic scripture (*śruti*). "Purified" means cleansed. Beginning with the instruction, "having poured the clarified butter (*ājya*) into the *ājyasthālī*," and continuing up to "having purified the clarified butter three times by moving it back and forth with two strainers (*pavitra*) whose tips point northward"—according to the procedure prescribed in the *Śāstra*, that clarified butter, which has been thus remembered, is like ghee (*sarpiḥ*); all of this becomes completely pure. By that [purification], may the waters not [defile] me.

The intended meaning is that [these mantras] all purify one from sin. Regarding the mantra employed for the offering of *arghya* during the midday *sandhyā*, he says: "Haṃsa. He is called *haṃsa* because he goes (*han*) through all living beings in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). The Supreme Self is named *haṃsa*;
the word "Sadāśiva" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. To the question of what kind of being he is, he says: "He sits, i.e., resides, in the pure moon."

Śuciṣat: According to the Śruti, "The Great Lord whose nature is the Moon, obeisance to the illustrious Mahādeva. Vasu: He in whom the world dwells; Rudra. According to the Śruti, "Everything was born in Me alone. Antarikṣasat: He who exists in the intermediate space; Ugra, whose nature is the Wind. According to the Śruti, "Obeisance to Ugra. Hotṛ: Paśupati, whose nature is the sacrificer. According to the Śruti, "He is the Lord of these; Paśupati is the Lord of creatures."

He who sits within the altar (*vedi*) is *vediṣat*. Rudra is of the nature of the sacrificial ladle (*vahni*), according to the Vedic revelation: "And for Rudra. At the time of worshipping Śiva, the guest (*atithi*) is Maheśvara himself, whose essence is Śiva. When such a guest has arrived as a result of one's meritorious deeds, one should worship that guest with a mind focused on the Lord, providing him with water, a seat, food, and other offerings, as well as drinks and pleasant words.

According to the statement in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*: "He who sits (*sīdati*) in dwellings (*duroṇeṣu*), that is, in houses, is *duroṇasat*," as per the Śruti: "And for the sake of the domestic [fire]. "He who sits among men (*nṛṣu*) in the form of the Self is *nṛṣat*," according to the Śruti: "Śiva alone is the God hidden in all beings; He is all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings. "He who sits in the best (*vare*), the most excellent, the witness of action (*karma-sākṣiṇi*), is *varasat*"; he whose nature is the Lord (*īśāna*).

Rudra; for the Śruti says, "The Lord (Īśāna) of all beings. He who sits (*sīdati*) as the protector in the sacrifice (*ṛta*) is Ṛtasat; Rudra, the protector of the sacrifice; for the Śruti says, "O kings, [come] to your sacrifice. He who sits in the void (*vyoman*), that is, in space (*ākāśa*), is Vyomasat; Rudra, whose nature is formidable (*bhīma*); for the Śruti says, "And to Bhīma. He who is born and abides in the waters (*ap*) is Abja; he whose nature is Bhava.

Rudra is [the deity] from the Vedic text: "Obeisance to Bhava. Gomā is Rudra in the form of Śarva, who is born and resides within cattle and the earth; this is from the Vedic text: "Obeisance to Śarva. Ṛtajā is Rudra, the protector of the Śiva-observance (samaya), who becomes manifest and remains present when there is a breach of vows such as the worship of Śiva; this is from the Vedic text: "Obeisance to Pulastya. He is the most observant of vows and is pure.

The intended meaning is that he is superior due to his devotion to the vows of Śiva as established by scripture. He is called *adrijā* because he is born and resides on the mountain (*adri*) Kailāsa; for there is a scriptural text stating, "Obeisance to Giriśa. Such is Sadāśiva, whose essence consists of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*).

The ritual of worshipping Śiva (*śivapūjākarma*), which consists of meditative worship (*upāsanātmaka*), is to be understood as the extensive and supreme *ruta*. This is to be known as the ritual of the worship of Śiva.
This is stated because of the *Kāmika* scripture’s teaching regarding external sacrifices and so forth; the word "having accomplished" (*sampādayitvā*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Now, prior to the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*, one should recite the single-syllabled Brahman, "Om," and likewise the *Gāyatrī* as the heart-verse (*hṛdaya*). Thus says Śaunaka:
"The single-syllabled Brahman, 'Om,' is called the heart; since it is the true foot of the *Gāyatrī*, one should perform the rite of recitation at the beginning."

That is now being explained: "Om, the single syllable. Om is the single syllable, Om is the single phoneme, according to the Śruti: "All is Rāma. Paraśiva is Brahman. Because of the statement, "You are the sheath of Brahman, covered by wisdom," there is an indication of the non-difference between the Praṇava and Śiva as the body and the embodied, or as the signifier and the signified. Due to being established in this very nature of the Praṇava, it is one; it is all-pervading.
The manner of the manifestation of the form "Oṃ" has been described; now it is stated by another method as taught in the *Prapañcasāra*, in the section on the creation of mantras:
"This mantra known as the Paramahaṃsa is declared to be 'So'ham' (I am That), together with 'Mā'."

When the prior conjunction (*pūrvasaṃdhi*) is made, the form "Oṃ" arises; for here, the letters *a*, *u*, and *m* are the constituent phonemes (*varṇaka*). Regarding the mantra called *paramahaṃsa*, which is "yo so 'ham" (*yo so 'ham*), when the letters *sa* and *ha* are elided and the prior conjunction is made, the form "Oṃ" arises—this is the meaning of the explanation. Furthermore, during meditation on Brahman, one should mutter the single-syllabled "Oṃ. As they say in that very same [text]: ("...")
Meditating on the single-syllable Brahman, "Om," the twice-born man should recite it;
having attained all his desires, he becomes fit for the realization of the reality of the Self.
In the scriptural passage beginning with "He who is the bull among the meters," which is applied to the section on recitation (*japa*),
all the secrets concerning its retention and so forth have been fully explained.

In that [verse], he indicates the seer and so forth: "Agni is the deity. Agni is the deity. The nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive; this is a Vedic usage [based on] the Śruti: "They consider Brahman to be the fourth, the auspicious non-duality. Thus, Brahman is Rudra. Regarding the seer (*ārṣa*), it means from the seer Rudra; the meaning is "of the seer" (*ṛṣeḥ*). This is based on the Śruti: "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to all. The meter is Gāyatrī.

The *gāyatrī* is the metre; the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the deity, meaning that Śiva is the deity in his essential form. The application (*viniyoga*) is for union (*sāyujya*), that is, for liberation (*mokṣa*). For it is stated in the Śruti: "At the departure of the breath of the creature, by this [mantra] he becomes immortal and attains liberation. This has been stated by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda: [The verse follows...]
Regarding the Praṇava, the Brahman-Ṛṣi is proclaimed, the metre is said to be Gāyatrī,
the deity is the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and it is employed for liberation and other such purposes.
In the *Śāradātilaka*:

"The Gāyatrī beginning with *brahma-daivī* is declared to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). The seers (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituent elements] of this [mantra], which is bowed to, have been proclaimed by the sages. Thus it is said.
