In the Vāmadeva-saṃhitā as well, it is stated: "The inner controller (antaryāmī) is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi); the deity is said to be the Gāyatra;
the supreme self, Śiva, is proclaimed to be its presiding divinity."

Now, regarding the statement, "Indeed, the single syllable 'ŪM' is Brahman," this is declared as a Ṛk; here, Gāyatrī is the heart, and that mantra is the color of the radiance of Gāyatrī. The single syllable 'ŪM' is the *kīla* (stake). Why has the word "Brahman" been added and expanded? It is true: as is Śiva, so is the Goddess; as is the Goddess, so is Śiva.
One should perceive no difference between these two, as between the moon and its reflection.

According to the statement, that which is of the nature of inseparable light and consists of Śiva and Śakti, expressed by the Gāyatrī or the Praṇava mantra, is the supreme reality whose essence is *vimarśa* (self-reflective awareness). As it is said in the *Śāradātilaka*:
"By the single syllable of the Praṇava, the partless Śiva is proclaimed."
Because it is the root mantra and because it serves as its substratum. In the Vāmadeva-saṃhitā:
"O God, that Mother who was previously described by You is most exalted...
O Rāma, they call that *praṇava* 'Mā'."

The essential meaning is this: by means of this [mantra], the *praṇava* which denotes Paraśiva, one performs the vow of invoking Paraśiva within the solar orb (*sauramaṇḍala*) existing in the heart-lotus (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*), having conceptualized it through the sixth [case-ending] and so forth. Now, he prays to Gāyatrī, the mother of all the Vedas, with the words "Come to me" (*āyāṃ tu*). She is the giver of boons (*varadā*); she is auspicious (*śivā*) because she bestows the desired fruits upon her worshippers; she is the giver of speech (*vāgadā*).

In the *Lalitāstotra*, [it says]: "O Mother, whose eyes grant boons, may Gāyatrī, who is the nature of the Mātṛkās and the form of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), come near me. This means: "May she, born from the thousand-petaled lotus, approach my presence.
To the question "What then? he replies: "The Imperishable" (*akṣaram*). The Imperishable is the form of the Root Nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) within the *praṇava*.

According to the *Kośa*, "tapasvinī" means "one whose nature is dharma"; according to the *Lalitāstotra*, she is "manifested from the root-prakṛti. The meaning is that Umā-Śakti has the Praṇava of Brahman as her essence. As stated in the *Śiva Purāṇa*:
"O Lord of Gods, O you who are saluted by all the gods, you alone are Śakti."
Your own *praṇava* as well as my own *praṇava*—
the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*— are mine.

"O Goddess, in your *praṇava*, the syllables *u*, *m*, and *a* are indeed sequentially submerged in three measures (*trimātrā*), and it is most excellent. It is measured as "I am" (*aham*) according to the authority of the Vedānta;
and she is the mother, the progenitor, of all the meters and of all the gods—the nominative case being used in the sense of the accusative.

The reading is Vedic. "Me" means in my heart (*hṛdayākāre*). According to the lexicon: "In *mājale*, in the vicinity, and in the sky, [it means] 'together'. O you who are adorned by the radiant lotus of the heart within the solar orb! O Self whose nature is the light of Brahman! O Supreme Śiva, graciously accept—be pleased with—this Gāyatrī, that is, this Consciousness-power (*cicchakti*) called Gāyatrī which is non-different from You.
In the Vāmadeva-saṃhitā it is said: "One should realize the Gāyatrī as non-different from Brahman;

one should meditate upon her with the thought 'I am she,' by whatever means possible. The form *ojaṣasvī* is a Vedic (chāndasa) form. This is because of the statement in the Vāyavya-saṃhitā: "O God who wields the thunderbolt, O wielder of the trident, the wind is indeed my beloved wife."

Because Śiva and Śakti are the supreme abode of the gods, he states the fruit of their worship: whatever sin one commits by day (*ahnat*), that nourishes [the self]; from the form of Śiva, one is liberated from that sin committed by day. From the night (*rātryāt*), whatever sin one commits during the night, that sin—[is liberated] by consciousness (*ciccha-*).

[He is] liberated from the night [of ignorance], which is of the nature of *kṛti* (action), according to the Śruti: "And for the sake of greater auspiciousness. By this, the meaning is that his worshiper is free from sin. Demonstrating the universal nature (*sarvātmakatva*) of the Gāyatrī, he praises her as the universal soul residing within the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-padma*), and then prays for her invocation with the words "O you of all colors" (*sarvavarṇe*). [This refers to her being the source] of all the powers (*śaktis*), such as the Ḍākinīs and others.

"Varṇāḥ" refers to colors such as red and so forth; it is an address to Her: "O Thou who art all colors! As it is said in the *Lalitāstotra*: "She who dwells upon the thousand-petaled lotus, adorned with all colors. "Mahādevī" means the Great Goddess, the consort of Mahādeva, the Supreme Brahman Sadāśiva; it is an address to Her: "O Mahādevī! "O Mahāmāyā, You cause the universe to wander [within] the Supreme Brahman."

O Śaṅkara, you have the Mahiṣī as your consort; O Sandhyā-vidyā, you who are the form of the twilight, O Parāśakti, you are autonomous (svacchanda). Indeed, she is the venerable Supreme Goddess herself, the deity of the twilight (sāṃdhyadevatā), Sarasvatī, whose nature consists of the fourfold speech beginning with Parā, according to the Vedic revelation: "Speech has been measured out in four quarters. O Goddess, you are born as the power of the senses; you are the companion, and you are the power that overcomes enemies.

You are *bala*, whose nature is the capacity of the body; you are *vrā*, whose nature is radiance (*jyotis*); you are the *dhāman*, the splendor of the gods such as Agni and others; you are the *vairya*, the valor of Brahmā and the other [deities]. As it is stated in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*: "Whatever power is proclaimed for each respective object..."
"She is that very Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe. You are the universe; you alone are the form of the world consisting of all that is moving.

The meaning is that the origin of the world, which consists of all that is moving, proceeds from you. You are the life-force of the entire expanse consisting of all that is stationary; you are time, whose essence is existence. [The stability] of the entire expanse consisting of all that is stationary [proceeds] from you.
The meaning is that [the world] comes into being. "Abhibhūḥ" refers to the dissolution (*pralaya*), which is the sublation of the entire phenomenal universe consisting of the mobile and immobile;

it proceeds from You, O *Obhavat* (O Source of Being), and not from anyone other than You. The fivefold cosmic activity beginning with creation does not originate from another. This is because the *Kośa* states: "Ūṃ is indeed the supreme thought. Likewise, it has been said in the *Lalitāstotra*: "She who creates is the form of Brahmā; she who protects is the form of Govinda."
"She is the withdrawer in the form of Rudra, the sovereign who effects concealment, Sadāśivā who bestows grace, and she whose ultimate goal is the fivefold cosmic function.

This is because of the statement: "The eternal Śakti, consisting of the three qualities, is established in Brahman. The sense is that the power of the Supreme Śakti is difficult for even the gods, including Brahmā, to comprehend. Now, having stated the invocation by means of names such as Gāyatrī and others, he examines the mantra.

The invocation of the Sandhyā-form of the Power of Consciousness (cicchakti), characterized by such attributes, is appropriate. However, the invocation of all four [deities], beginning with Gāyatrī, is indeed impossible. Therefore, in the Āgamas, there is the invocation of only one—the Sandhyā-form of the Power of Consciousness. The other deities, Gāyatrī and the rest, are to be worshipped as being identical with the Praṇava. As it has been said:
In the *Śāradātilaka*, regarding the occasion of the worship of Gāyatrī:
"Having prepared a mandala with a radiant pericarp in the shape of a triangle, the wise man should worship there upon the solar seat (saurapīṭha) with the nine powers beginning with Dīptā."
"One should worship the Goddess in embodied form once she has been awakened by the root mantra;
having worshipped [the deities] in the three corners, one should worship the powers beginning with Brahmā on the outside.
Here, the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is the nature of *sandhyā*, indeed assumes various forms. As it is stated in the *Vāyavīya Saṃhitā*:
Nor is there another power of the nature of consciousness characterized by productivity;
rather, having divided the universe manifoldly and established it by the will of Śiva.
She is the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), Māyā, possessed of the three qualities (triguṇā), and is remembered as being threefold;
by her this entire universe, from Śiva down to the earth, is pervaded.
Indeed, powers are divided in many ways according to conventional usage— into one, three, and likewise into hundreds of thousands.
"The Raudrī power is that of Rudra; the Vaiṣṇavī is considered to be that of Viṣṇu;
the Brahmāṇī is declared to be that of Brahmā; and the Aindrī is said to be that of Indra," and so forth.

Therefore, the consciousness-power (cicchakti) whose form is the twilight (sandhyā) belongs to the One [Brahman], yet her invocation is twofold, through the distinction between the external and the internal.

Within this [space], in the circle of the solar orb adorned with the lotus of the heart, upon the lap of Sadāśiva invoked within that solar mandala, one should invoke Gāyatrī by means of the invocation of the Ṛṣis and other elements as will be described. Because she protects those who sing (*gāyantaṃ*) until the end, she is called Gāyatrī; thus, Sāvitrī, whose form is such Gāyatrī, is proclaimed as Sāvitrī because she is the radiance (*dyotana*) of the Sun (*savituḥ*).

Thus, having performed the invocation of the *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, and so forth for Sarasvatī—who is of the nature of Sāvitrī, or who is called Sarasvatī because she brings forth (*prasavitṛ*) the world—he performed the invocation with the root mantra externally; the word "in the image" (*mūrtau*) is to be supplied as the remainder. [He likewise invoked] Śrī, who is mixed with these [mantras] of Gāyatrī—that is, Mahālakṣmī, whose form is the twilight (*sandhyā*).
Having meditated on the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) as coral (vidruma), one says, "I invoke. By this, the gesture of invocation (āvāhanamudrā) is indicated.

Through the four previously mentioned words beginning with "I invoke," the four gestures starting with installation (sthāpanā) are described. It is clearly stated in the Śivapurāṇa that she who is the Supreme Power, O Śiva, is Mahālakṣmī. As it is said: [The text continues with the verse: "O Śiva, she who is the Supreme Power is indeed Mahālakṣmī..."
Upon that [lotus] is mounted the supreme Śakti of Maheśvara, the auspicious Mahālakṣmī;
she is that which is "All this, O Pervasive One."

In the *Lalitāstotra*, she is called Mahādevī, Māheśvarī, Mahālakṣmī, and the beloved of Mṛḍa. Also in the *Vādhūla-saṃhitā*, it is said: "They call her Śrī, Lakṣmī, Aupalā, Ambikā, Gā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Jayā, and Indrasenā"—so says the Śruti. Furthermore, the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda has also stated that she is Turīyā, as follows: [text follows].
Those who know the scriptures call her the Goddess of Speech, the consort of Brahmā;
they call her Padmā, the wife of Hari; and they call her the daughter of the Mountain, the companion of Hara.
She is the fourth [state], the essence of all beings, whose boundless majesty is difficult to comprehend.
"O Mahāmāyā, consort of the Supreme Brahman, you cause the universe to revolve.
Thus [it is said]. Now, he shows the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [components] for the Gāyatrī, beginning with the words "of the Gāyatrī. For the Gāyatrī mantra, the meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī;
the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Viśvāmitra—the one who destroyed the immeasurable (the demon) Vītra; that is to say, the seer is Rudra. The deity (*devatā*) is Savitṛ; the mouth is Agni.

Brahmā is the head; Viṣṇu is the heart; Rudra is the crest-lock (śikhā); the Earth is the base (yoni). She consists of the five vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna; this is the meaning. Endowed with these vital breaths and accompanied by the secondary breaths known as Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya, she is white in color. She is Vaiṣṇavī, Sarasvatī, Īśānī, and Rudrāṇī.

Sāvitrī is to be known as white in color. Her lineage is Sāṃkhyāyana; that is, she belongs to the same lineage as a certain ṛṣi named Sāṃkhyāyana. The term Gāyatrī has already been explained. Everything was previously stated at the time of the invocation. Twenty increased by four is twenty-four; she is one who possesses that many syllables.

She consists of twenty-four syllables. She is "three-footed" (tripadā), meaning she is endowed with three feet in the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. She is "six-bellied" (ṣaṭkukṣiḥ), meaning she whose bellies are the six powers (śaktis) beginning with Ḍākinī. She is "five-headed" (pañcaśīrṣā), [meaning she whose heads are] the five [faces] beginning with Sadyojāta.

She whose heads are named Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna is "Pañcaśīrṣā" (the Five-headed One). Having performed the visualization (*dhyāna*) with faces possessing the lusters of pearl, coral, sapphire, gold, and white, everything regarding the dream has been stated. Regarding the *upanayana*: it is the leading (*nayana*) or bringing (*ānayana*) near to Śiva; the application (*niyoga*) is in that [rite]. Everything [is to be done] previously at the time of the invocation (*āvāhana*).

It is prepared. Having meditated upon the Supreme Śiva, who resides in the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) as the Gāyatrī in the form of the power of consciousness (cicchakti), the recitation (japa) should be performed;

this is the meaning. The meaning of the syllables of the mantra for the evening worship (sāyam-upasthāna) is now explained. Regarding the word "imam" (this): according to the Śruti, "vārivastvatāya," O Varuṇa—Rudra whose nature is Varuṇa—in the Vāmadeva-saṃhitā:
"With the mantra *imaṃ me*, one should worship Śiva as the most excellent (*varuṣṭham*). Thus [it is said]. "Hear (*śrudhi*)"—that is, listen to—this my speech, this invocation (*āhvānam*).

The sense is: "Listen to the invocation in the form of a prayer. What is the purpose of that hearing? To answer that, he says: "Make it cease" (*kṣayāma*). Another [reading] is *arghe vā naḥ*; the lengthening of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasaḥ*). "Be gracious" (*mṛḍaya*), that is, make us happy; [release us from] the bondage of birth and so forth.

"Parihṛtyamam" means "and make me happy. Regarding "tvām": "I, desiring protection (avasyuḥ)—that is, desiring my own preservation (avanam)—long for you, the Blessed One, as my protector; I desire [you]. It is not merely a matter of longing; rather, preceded by praise, he says "tat," meaning "to that [end]," indicating that he has come for refuge. The elision of the case-ending (*vibhakti-lopa*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*). The meaning is: "for the sake of protection. [This refers to] Brahmā.

Praising with a mantra consisting of hymns, he offers salutation while bowing; "I approach you" (tvā yāguprāpyo). According to the Śruti: "O Giriśa, we invoke you with auspicious speech. Since you are the protector of your devotees, I therefore take refuge in you, worshiping you alone as my guardian.
I am [your servant]; therefore, have mercy on me. The implication is that otherwise, the abandonment of one who has come for refuge would be a great fault.

Regarding the word *yajamāna*: the sacrificer (*yaṣṭṛ*), the worshipper, with the offerings (*haviḥ*)—that is, with the food and other items dedicated for your sake as instruments—seeks and prays for your sprinkling (*abhiṣeka*). Therefore, the meaning is: "May you be happy in this state. [With] *tvādaṃtebhiḥ*...

According to the Śruti, "With these most peaceful Rudras... [it says], "O non-disdainful one" (*aheḍamāna*). O Rudra, whose nature is Varuṇa: being *aheḍamāna*, that is, not showing contempt, at this time when you are present, perceive my prayer. *Uruśaṃsa*—one who is to be praised with many mantras; his address is *uru śaṃsa*. His name is *uru-kīrti*, meaning "of great fame. [May] his protection (*sena*) [grant] us long life (*āyuḥ*).

"Do not steal our life; do not destroy it. The meaning is: "Grant us the longevity declared in the Vedas. Regarding the word *yat*: *cit* and *hi* are two particles used for the purpose of filling out the meter (*pādapūraṇa*). O Varuṇa—O Rudra whose nature is Varuṇa—that vow which consists of the meditation on this [truth], we consider it to be most excellent (*pramanīyasī*) day by day (*dyavidyavi*), that is, every single day. In that regard...

The illustration is as follows: just as common people (*viśaḥ*) perform their respective duties, even so do we always deliberate upon our own actions; therefore, we serve you alone. "Whatever" (*yat kiṃca*): O Varuṇa—meaning, within you, who are of the nature of Rudra and reside in the divine world—whatever slight or great offense (*droha*) we have committed through thoughtlessness (*acitti*), [we acknowledge]. (**) *Citti*: through lack of awareness. (**) *Droha*: an offense, whether small or great.

We move about and act as ignorant men; moreover, O Deva Rudra, who is Varuṇa, although your work is long (dharma being a Vedic form for *dharmam*), we destroy even that which is yours within me. Therefore, from this sin—that is, from this malice—may he protect us in this [world].

"O great ones, having avoided the sin of neglecting the ritual act, protect us"—this is the meaning. Furthermore, those who are like gamblers, intent on achieving their own selfish ends, have harmed—that is, destroyed—the limb of the ritual. O Goddess, they do not proceed correctly when the rite is being performed. Or else, the two indeclinables *uta* and *iti* indicate an alternative view and serve as verse-fillers.
The particles *vā*, *apavā*, and *ca* are indeclinables (*nipāta*). Alternatively, "that which" refers to that which is true; it has necessarily been done. The meaning is: "done as if unknowingly.
"That which is below" (*yad adhaḥ*)—and furthermore (*uta*), that which is the very nature of Dharma, meaning neither obstacle nor birth. Let it be so; what is there [in that]? He says: "all," etc.
All things, all those which have been heard by us in many ways, they desire this [state]. Having entered into all of them, [he remains] in this.

"Make them depart especially from our presence"—the meaning is "destroy them. Having thus desired the removal of major sins (*pātaka*), he now desires the removal of minor sins (*upapātaka*): "loosen [them] indeed, loosen [them]"—this is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Another [commentator] says: "loosen all those which are minor sins. Then, after your terrifying glance, O Varuṇa—O God Rudra whose nature is Varuṇa—[grant us protection]. (**) Note: The text fragment *te* refers to the deity being addressed. The phrase *bhayavat-kaṭākṣānantaram* indicates that this follows the description of the Lord's fierce side-glance. The term *varuṇātmaka* identifies Rudra with Varuṇa, the lord of the waters and the remover of sin. The repetition of *śithira* (loosen) emphasizes the intensity of the plea for release from bondage. The reading *viśya* is interpreted as *viśīrya* (having shattered or loosened). The final portion of the text implies a transition from the fear of the divine gaze to a prayer for mercy and purification.
May we be dear, may we not be unloved.
He states the mantra for the morning worship: "Of Mitra... [The verse begins: "Of Mitra," who is of the nature of the Sun, "the *carṣaṇyaḥ*" are his rays;
"of those, the supporter of the people (*carṣaṇidhṛt*). Of that god Rudra, "fame" (*śravaḥ*) is that which is heard—his glory, which is "winning" (*sānasi*), meaning worthy of being properly shared.

His name is "Mahadyaśas" (of great fame), according to the Vedic revelation; the meaning is that one must perform the remembrance of Śiva’s name alone. It is "satyam" (true) because it is indestructible, and "citram" (wondrous) because it is heard with such excellence as to be marvelous; thus, it is "vastamam" (most excellent), meaning it brings happiness to those who hear it. "Aṅkuṃ" refers to Rudra in the form of the Sun, the friend. Knowing—that is, being aware of their respective offices—he impels all people toward their own [duties].

He appoints each to its own duty. Moreover, Mitra—Rudra in his solar aspect—upheld both the earth and the heavens. And Mitra, Rudra in his solar aspect, oversees all people (*kṛṣṭīḥ*)—that is, humans—and the "unblinking" (*animiṣāḥ*), the awakened gods; the loss of the case-ending is a Vedic archaism. He watches over all.

He beholds; the meaning is that he illuminates everything. To him who is truth, whose fruit is unfailing, or whose very self is truth—to that Rudra in the form of a friend—we offer the oblation (*havya*) characterized by the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, accompanied by clarified butter (*ghṛtavat*).
O Ādityas, through your connection with his sacred vow (*vrata*), the sacrificer is able to perform the ritual; he becomes capable of its execution.

Having performed the *nyāsa* of the other [deities] and having placed Śambhu himself upon his own heart with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, he should wrap the triple-thread (*trisūtrī*) around his neck with the *kavaca-mantra*. Having established the two auspicious vessels on the left side with the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*), he should worship them with sandalwood paste, flowers, and so forth. Then, taking cow's clarified butter (*gavyamājya*) that has been purified by the four rites beginning with *nirīkṣaṇa* and is contained within a vessel of ghee—

Then, having contemplated one’s own body as consisting of Brahman, and having taken a vessel of clarified butter and heated it three times over the fire above the *kuṇḍa* within the range of vision, one should place it in the southeast. Taking a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a blade of *darbha* grass, one should offer it into the fire with the mantra: "Oṃ Hāṃ, svāhā to Brahman.
Then, meditating on one’s own body as consisting of Viṣṇu, one should [place] the vessel of clarified butter in the northeast corner by way of circumambulation.

Having placed a drop of clarified butter on the tip of a *kuśa* blade and offered it with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ [to] Pauṣṭika (Viṣṇu) svāhā," one should then meditate upon one's own body as consisting of Rudra. Having circumambulated the vessel of clarified butter and cast it into the womb of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should offer a drop of clarified butter on the tip of a *kuśa* blade with the mantra "Ūṃ huṃ ūṃ hūṃ [to] Rudra svāhā. Thereafter—
Having taken with the thumb and ring finger a *pavitra* made from two tips of *darbha* grass, measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length and having a knot in the middle,

one should stir the clarified butter three times in front of the fire with the *astra-mantra*. Likewise, having performed a sprinkling in front of oneself with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should untie the knot of that *pavitra*.

Having sprinkled it with water, one should cast it into the fire. Having consecrated a burnt *darbha* brand with the *Hṛdaya-mantra* and having thrown it into clarified butter while reciting the *Astra-mantra*, one should purify it and cast that glowing [brand] into the mouth of the fire. Having performed the *nīrājana* rite with another flaming *darbha* while reciting the *Kavaca-mantra*, one should cast it into the fire. Having shaken another *darbha* with the *Astra-mantra*, one should cast that brand into the fire. Then, [taking] a piece of wood one span long...

Having placed the *pavitra*—made from two tips of *darbha* grass with a central knot—into the midst of the clarified butter while reciting the *praṇava*, one should distinguish the two fortnights, the bright and the dark, by means of the right and left [paths]. Then, having conceived the triad of channels—*piṅgalā*, *iḍā*, and *suṣumnā*—in the right, left, and middle portions respectively, one should take clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle from the right side and offer it, saying: *Oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā*.

Thus, having offered a small portion into the mouth of the fire with the mantra "Ūṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā," one should offer into the right eye of the fire with "Ūṃ hāṃ somāya svāhā" after taking clarified butter from the left part;
into the left eye of the fire with "Ūṃ hāṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ gūṃ svāhā" after taking clarified butter from the middle part; and into the middle eye of the fire [with the same].
Then, having taken clarified butter from all three parts and offered a little into the mouth of the fire with "Ūṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā," [the rite is complete].

One should cast the remaining clarified butter into the *ājyabhāga* offerings with the mantra "svāhā. However, during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), having visualized the three channels—Piṅgalā, Iḍā, and Suṣumnā—in the right, left, and middle portions respectively, one should take clarified butter from the left portion with the *sruva* ladle and offer it to the fire in the left eye with "Ūṃ Hāṃ Agnaye Svāhā"; then, taking clarified butter from the right portion, [one offers it] to Sūrya...

Saying "svāhā," one takes clarified butter from the middle portion and offers it into the southern eye of the fire with "oṃ hāṃ agni-sūryābhyāṃ gūṃ svāhā. Taking clarified butter from three portions, one offers it into the middle eye of the fire with "oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā. Having taken a small amount for the mouth of the fire, one should cast the remaining clarified butter into those portions of the fire with "svāhā."

Having consecrated the ghee with the six-limbed mantra and transformed it into nectar using the root mantra and the *dhenumudrā*, one should protect it with the *astra* mantra and veil it with the *kavaca* mantra. By sprinkling drops of clarified butter with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should purify the remaining ghee. Then, for the purpose of pouring it over the faces, one should [offer] *sadyādi* and so forth upon the five faces, beginning with *ūṃ hāṃ sadyojātāya*.

*Svāhā*. *Ūṃ hāṃ vāmadevāya svāhā*. *Ūṃ huṃ aghorāya svāhā*. *Ūṃ hūṃ tatpuruṣāya svāhā*. *Ūṃ heṃ īśānāya svāhā*. One should offer oblations, either individually one by one or collectively with three oblations.
Then, for the purpose of joining the faces: *Ūṃ hāṃ hiṃ sadyojāta-vāmadevābhyāṃ gūṃ svāhā*. *Ūṃ hiṃ...*

HŪṂ VĀMADEVA-AGHORĀBHYĀṂ GŪṂ SVĀHĀ | ŪṂ HUṂ HEṂ AGHORA-TATPURUṢĀBHYĀṂ GŪṂ SVĀHĀ | ŪṂ HEṂ HEṂ TATPURUṢEŚĀNĀBHYĀṂ GŪṂ SVĀHĀ | ŪṂ HEṂ ĪŚĀNĀYA SVĀHĀ | One should offer oblations with these three mantras one by one, or with each individually. Then, for the purpose of unifying the faces: ŪṂ HAṂ HĀṂ HAṂ HEṂ HEṂ.

One should offer oblations of clarified butter in an unbroken stream from the fire toward the wind, proceeding through the directions starting from the southwest (Nairṛti) with the mantra: "Svāhā to Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna. Alternatively, according to the root text:
"Whatever the desired measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should contemplate its faces; the other faces are included within it, and this is considered the method of unification."

Having visualized the face of Śiva in the center of the *kuṇḍa*, one recites: "In that [face], *ūṃ hāṃ hiṃ huṃ heṃ hāṃ*, svāhā to Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna. This is considered the Vīraśaiva position, according to the statement: "I always offer oblations into the fire of Rudra, which is the Supreme Brahman consisting of the six *sthala*s"; thus, it consists of the six *sthala*s.

"Śivāgni" refers to the Vīraśaiva Siddhānta. Now, for the purpose of designating the tongues [of the fire], [one offers oblations] to the seven tongues beginning with Hiraṇyā, situated in their respective directions: *yrūṃ* to Hiraṇyā, Svāhā, in the west; *kanakāyai* Svāhā, in the center of the fire;
*plūṃ* to Raktā, Svāhā, in the north; *śrūṃ* to Kṛṣṇā, Svāhā, in the south; and *ghrāṃ* to Suprabhā, Svāhā.

To the east: *srūṃ* to Atirikti, *svāhā*. To the center: *haṃ* to Bahurūpā, *svāhā*. Having thus offered one oblation each separately, he should then offer for the purpose of joining the tongues: *yrūṃ brāṃ* to Hiraṇya and Kanaka, *gūṃ svāhā*; *prūṃ śrūṃ* to Rakta and Kṛṣṇā, *gūṃ svāhā*; *śrūṃ ghrāṃ* to Kṛṣṇa and Suprabhā, *gūṃ svāhā*.

*Ghrāṃ srūṃ*, to Suprabhā and Atiraktā, *gūṃ svāhā*. *Srūṃ hrūṃ*, to Atirikta and Bahurūpā, *gūṃ svāhā*. Now, for the purpose of unifying the tongues: *yrūṃ lrū prūṃ śrūṃ ghrāṃ srūṃ hrūṃ*, to Hiraṇya, Kanaka, Rakta, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Atiraktā, and Bahurūpā, *gūṃ svāhā*. [Thus it is said] in the mouth of Śiva.

In the preceding rite, one should offer oblations with an uninterrupted stream of clarified butter; this is the *jātakarman*. Then, for the purpose of naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), having worshipped with the *Īśāna* mantra, and having performed the naming of the fire with the *astra* mantra by offering three oblations of sesame seeds—reciting "O Śiva-fire, you are the consumer of oblations" (*hutāśana*)—and having worshipped Vāgīśī and Vāgīśvara at the heart with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should dismiss them both while reciting the *kumbhaka* [breath-retention].

Having visualized the face of Śiva, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* for the sake of pleasing the consecrations such as the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) and the tonsure (*cūḍā*). It is as follows: having filled the *sruc* ladle with clarified butter using the *Pañcabrahma* mantra, and having placed the *sruva* spoon within it facing upward, one should place a flower at the tip of the *sruc*.

Then, holding those two with the left hand and again with the right hand in the *śaṅkha-sannibha* mudrā, rising with feet together and body straight, turning his gaze slightly sideways toward his own navel, or else fixing his sight on the tip of the *sruk*, he should recite the root mantra ending in *ṣaṭ* (svāhā) until the end of the *pluta* prolation,
while holding the *sruk* and *sruva*.

Having led the base of the two [channels] sequentially to the tip of the left nostril with streams of clarified butter, while recollecting the stream of nectar issuing from the *bindu* through the *suṣumṇā* by means of the sequential abandonment of the causal deities beginning with Brahmā,

one should offer all the clarified butter into the fire with a continuous stream of the *pramāṇa* mantra; having thus performed the *pūrṇāhuti* and sat down, [one should meditate on the deity] who is red and endowed with five faces.
Adorned with seven tongues of flame, possessing ten arms and three eyes, and decorated with all ornaments.
Clad in red garments, seated upon a lotus,
sitting in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), and equipped with the goad as his weapon.
Kanaka, Bahurūpā, and Atiriktā beyond that;
Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, Raktā, and another, Hiraṇmayī.

"The three [lines] are situated with their faces upward; the remaining ones are situated starting from the east. Having thus meditated upon the Śiva-fire (—), one should request the command as follows: "O Fire, since you are sovereignty, splendor, and the supreme means of purification, therefore, having established you within the lotus of my heart, I shall satisfy you. Thus, one should pray for the command.

Having recollected, "I have entered within the body of the Lord through the Suṣumnā channel," one should worship the radiant Lord— along with His faces, limbs, and enclosures— in His heart-lotus as before, using perfumes and other offerings. Then, having joined the mouth of Śiva with the mouth of fire and united it with oneself, and having performed the ritual of extraction (niṣkṛti), at the time of the food offering (naivedya), [one should offer] to Śiva with the root mantra.

Having offered ten oblations to the others and one single oblation to the principal deity, and having performed the *tarpaṇa* by offering one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra—or a tenth part thereof—to Brahmā and the other deities; having performed the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as previously described, sat down, sipped water (*ācamana*), and offered betel-leaf and other gifts; having attained [the deity’s] grace through devotion and prostrated, one should perform the ritual of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).

One should burn the four enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) soaked in ghee with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and the four layers of grass (*paristaraṇa*) soaked in ghee with the *vastra-mantra*. However, in the daily ritual (*nityakarman*), one should consecrate each of the enclosing sticks with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and each of the layers of grass with the *astra-mantra* five times; both of these [sets] likewise.

He should dismiss [the deities]. Then, having touched the tips of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the tips of the *darbha* blades placed in their respective portions—having touched the middle with the middle and the base with the base—he should release them. Having cast the *darbha* blades that touched the parts of the *sruk* and *sruva* into the fire with the *kavaca* mantra, he should take up the *viṣṭara* grass mats, untie the knots, and dismiss them. Then, having untied the triple-strand binding with the *kavaca* mantra...

Having set aside the vessel for clarified butter (*ājya*), one should take the remainder of the *ājya* and, with the *astra-mantra*, pour it onto the ground in the southwest (*nairṛtya*) for the satisfaction of the *rākṣasa*s and other spirits. Then, having worshipped the fire and withdrawn it by means of the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*) using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should establish the Śiva-fire within the lotus of the heart. Thereafter, having prepared two mandalas—the *kuṭāga* and the *vināga*—in the first mandala...

From the east to the north: *ūṃ hāṃ rudrebhyo namaḥ* | *ūṃ hāṃ mātṛbhyo namaḥ* | *ūṃ hāṃ gaṇebhyo namaḥ* | *ūṃ hāṃ yakṣebhyo namaḥ*. In the corners from the northeast to the northwest: *ūṃ hāṃ grahebhyo namaḥ* | *ūṃ hāṃ asurebhyo namaḥ* | *ūṃ hāṃ rakṣasebhyo namaḥ* | *ūṃ hāṃ*.
Homage to the Nāgas. Within the mandala, in the corners starting from Īśāna and ending at Vāyavya: *ūṃ hāṃ* homage to the constellations (*nakṣatra*);

*ūṃ hāṃ* homage to the zodiac signs (*rāśi*); *ūṃ hāṃ* homage to the Yakṣas; *ūṃ hāṃ* homage to the Viśvedevas. Between Vāyu and Varuṇa, having worshipped with "homage to Kṣetrapāla," ending with *svāhā*.
Having offered the *bali* oblation, one should dismiss them. In the second maṇḍala, in the eight directions starting from the east and ending with the northeast: (—) *ūṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*;
*ūṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*; *ūṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*; *ūṃ hāṃ nirṛtaye namaḥ*; *ūṃ hāṃ*...

Salutation to Varuṇa. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Vāyu. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Kubera. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Īśāna. In the northeast, *ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Brahmā; in the west, salutation to Viṣṇu. Having worshipped in the center with "salutation to Nīlalohita," and having offered the *bali* ending with *svāhā*, [one should say]: "I shall prepare the Śiva-fire in the south-east."

Having resolved upon the performance of the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), being provided with all necessary implements, and having obtained permission from Śiva for the sake of the fire-rite, he should take the fire-vessel and other required items. Having approached either a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a leveled altar (*sthaṇḍila*) prepared in one of the directions— south, southwest, or northwest— and having sat down facing either east or north, [he should perform the rite] in the pit or on the altar.
Having prepared three lines with their tips pointing east using kusha grass by means of the middle mantra, one should then prepare a line with its tip pointing north.
Having prepared it in reverse order from that, having sprinkled it with the armor-mantra (kavaca), and having visualized the perfection of all purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*),
one should meditate there upon Śyāmā, who is in her menses, adorned with fine garments, garlands, and ornaments, and possessing a serene countenance, [seated] upon a lotus petal.

Having meditated thus on the three eyes, and having meditated upon that god Vāgīśvara with the mantra "Oṃ Hrīṃ Vāgīśvaryai Namaḥ," and having worshipped him with "Oṃ Hāṃ Vāgīśvarāya Namaḥ" and offered the *arghya*,

one should thereafter bring fire— either produced from a fire-drill (*araṇi*) or from a pure hearth— into a clean vessel; then, having discarded the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyād*), one performs the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth.

Having consecrated with the four purificatory rites (saṃskāras), one should take up the fire by means of the *saṃhāramudrā* with the mantra "Oṃ Hrāṃ Rāṃ, obeisance to the form of Fire" (*vahnimūrtaye namaḥ*). Drawing it in through inhalation (*pūraka*), uniting it with the abdominal fire (*nābhyagni*) and the lunar fire (*baiṇdava*) during retention (*kumbhaka*), and merging them into one, one should [exhale] through the *piṅgalā* channel during exhalation (*recaka*).

Having established [the fire] with the fire-mantra, "Ūṃ hāṃ rāṃ, obeisance to the form of fire," which resembles the flame of a lamp, using the seed-syllable of fire and the *udbhava-mudrā*; having worshipped it with its associated *saṃhitā* and contemplated it as the virility of the Supreme Lord; and having visualized Vāgīśvarī being cast into the womb-channel by Vāgīśvara—

Having placed [the image] facing oneself with the *mūla-mantra*, having swept [the area], having clothed the Goddess, and having offered purification, water for rinsing the mouth, and so forth with the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
having worshipped with the *brahmans* beginning with Sadyojāta; and having offered five oblations with the *mūla-mantra*;
[one should worship] in the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; Oṃ..."

Hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra; Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśvara—having thus worshipped, [one should worship] in the eight directions from the east to the northeast: Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra; Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni; Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Yama; Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nairṛti; Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa; Ūṃ...

Hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyu. Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kubera. Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Pointing toward the upper region in the northeast: Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā. Pointing toward the lower region in the southwest: Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu. Having thus worshipped and requested protection for the fire, [one says]: Ūṃ hauṃ, you are the Śiva-fire.

Having performed the naming ceremony of the fire as "Hutāśana," one should release the sacrificial vessels (*pitakā*). Then, having worshipped Śiva—who consists of the five Brahmans—within the heart-lotus of the fire, one should offer oblations according to one's capacity with clarified butter using the root mantra and the Brahma-aṅga mantras in ten parts.
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should offer the *caru* for the food offering (*naivedya*), and then offer water for sipping (*ācamana*), betel-leaf, and so forth.

Having worshipped with those ashes in the fire using the *aṣṭapuṣpikā* offering and having offered the *bali* to Brahmā and the others, one should prepare two mandalas on one's own right side. In the first mandala, in the four directions starting from the east: *Ūṃ hāṃ rudrebhyo namaḥ*. *Ūṃ hāṃ*...
Salutation to the Mothers. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Gaṇas. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Yakṣas.

In the four directions beginning with the northeast (*īśāna*): *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Planets (*graha*). *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Asuras. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Rākṣasas. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the Nāgas. In the four corners of the center of the mandala beginning with the northeast: *Ūṃ*.

Hāṃ, obeisance to the constellations. Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the zodiac signs. Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Yakṣas. Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Viśvedevas. Between Vāyu and Varuṇa, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla. Having thus worshipped and offered the bali and arghya ending with *svāhā*, [one should worship] in the eight directions beginning with the east within the second maṇḍala: Ūṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra. Ūṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to Agni. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Yama. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Nirṛti. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Varuṇa. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Vāyu. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Kubera. *Ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Īśāna. In the northeast, *ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Brahmā. In the southwest, *ūṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Viṣṇu. In the center, salutation to Nīlalohita.

Having thus worshipped, and having offered the *bali* and the *arghya* ending with *svāhā*, one should dismiss the previously mentioned Rudras and others. Having thus prepared the *śivāgni*, one should perform the *aupāsana* and the *vaiśvadeva* rites, preceded by the *mahābhāga-hantakāra*, according to the statement in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā*: "The *vaiśvadeva* and so forth, preceded by the *mahābhāga-hantakāra*. It is as follows: having performed *prāṇāyāma*, [at] evening...
In the morning, I shall offer oblations with *taṇḍula* rice at the *aupāsana* fire.
[I meditate upon the Fire-god] who is endowed with five faces, red in color, resplendent with seven tongues of flame,
possessing ten hands and three eyes, and adorned with all ornaments.
Clad in red garments and seated upon a lotus.
Seated in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), endowed with the ten weapons;
then, respectively, Kanakā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā.
Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, Raktā, and another which is golden.
Three are situated facing upwards; the remaining ones are positioned starting from the east.
Having thus meditated upon the Śivāgni and having sprinkled it with water while reciting the Gāyatrī, [one should worship with: Ūṃ, obeisance to Jātavedas;
Ūṃ, obeisance to Saptajihva; Ūṃ, obeisance to Havyavāhana; Ūṃ, obeisance to Aśvodaraja; Ūṃ, obeisance to Vaiśvānara.
